**Summary.** This paper details the design and optimization of reversible quantum circuits for elliptic-curve point addition, a key component of quantum factoring algorithms. By employing advanced record-and-replay techniques, the authors significantly reduce the required quantum resources compared to existing methods. The work provides valuable insights into implementing complex, large-scale arithmetic operations on quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on number theory algorithms, the techniques developed for minimizing quantum gate counts and managing reversible state evolution (record-and-replay) are highly relevant to optimizing any complex quantum circuit implementation, including those for simulating quantum many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper focuses on developing highly efficient, reversible quantum circuits for performing elliptic-curve point addition, a critical subroutine for Shor's algorithm.

**Main result.** The authors present and compare three optimized record-and-replay constructions (Jump-2, ping-pong, fused replay) that achieve resource savings for windowed point addition compared to baseline methods.

**Method.** The core method involves adapting record-and-replay quantum arithmetic techniques, utilizing specialized encoding (base-5) and fixed-schedule register alternation to minimize quantum resources.

**Model / system.** The model is quantum computation implemented using reversible gates, specifically targeting arithmetic on the secp256k1 elliptic curve over a finite field. The circuits are designed to perform point addition in an 'in-place' manner to conserve quantum workspace.

**Key observables.** Resource costs measured in qubits (e.g., 1,151 logical qubits) and mean executed Toffolis (e.g., 1.356 million). Diagnostics include failure counts, phase flag counts, and trace distance bounds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is constrained by the window size allowance and compares resource usage against established low-gate caps from prior literature.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results are limited to individual window-selected additions, not complete Shor computations, and formal dominance over prior work is not established due to differing accounting methods.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the multi-stage pipelines of the Jump-2 mixed-addition circuit, while algorithms detail the record phase for modular inverse calculation using Dialog-GCD.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the need for efficient in-place arithmetic, detailing the record-and-replay framework, presenting and optimizing three distinct constructions (Jump-2, ping-pong, fused replay), and concluding with rigorous resource comparisons and error analysis.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits developed through ECDSA.Fail for Shor's elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm algorithm. Two complementary constructions improve record-and-replay GCD arithmetic: Jump-2 groups binary-GCD steps and compresses their decisions using base-5 encoding, while ping-pong uses fixed register alternation and one-bit decisions to avoid full-width comparisons and data-dependent swaps. Fused replay combines doubling and signed addition into one modular correction. Both constructions support quantum-addressed window selection with measurement-based lookup cleanup. We compare three circuits on 100,000 fresh inputs across nine lookup-table configurations. A separately tested repair uses 1,419 qubits and 1.356 million mean executed Toffolis, with no detected failures on another 100,000 inputs. Structured supported-input counterexamples remain, so these tests do not establish all-input correctness. We also provide conditional coherent-error analysis and reversible safegcd comparisons. Under the stated window allowance, repaired-circuit resources lie below Google's low-gate caps and Schrottenloher's low-gate estimates, but differing accounting and correctness evidence preclude formal dominance. The results concern individual window-selected additions, not complete Shor computations.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces Learned-Projector QAOA (LP-QAOA), a novel multistage quantum algorithm designed to solve combinatorial optimization problems with hierarchical structure. It improves upon standard QAOA by freezing optimized intermediate states to define subsequent mixers, which enhances the ability to sample the true ground state. The results demonstrate that LP-QAOA is superior to existing methods on structured test cases.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of using learned projectors to guide quantum optimization by exploiting problem structure is highly relevant for developing scalable quantum algorithms beyond simple local Hamiltonians.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of improving variational quantum optimization for combinatorial problems that possess inherent hierarchical structure.

**Main result.** The proposed Learned-Projector QAOA (LP-QAOA) outperforms tested baselines by achieving higher probabilities of sampling the optimum and lower estimated resource requirements on structured instances.

**Method.** LP-QAOA is a multistage protocol that recursively uses the optimized state from an earlier stage to define a projector mixer for subsequent stages, ensuring structural information is progressively incorporated.

**Model / system.** The method is tested on Block-Constrained Spin Tiling (BCST) instances and Stochastic Block Model (SBM) graphs, which model constrained optimization problems. The core mechanism involves defining a mixer based on the projection onto a previously optimized quantum state.

**Key observables.** Probability of sampling the unique optimum ($P_{	ext{succ}}$), total estimated cost (Resource Units), and gradient magnitudes for training convergence.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The depth of the QAOA circuit (number of stages/layers) and the structure of the hierarchy (strict vs. soft).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The stability theorem provides bounds on error propagation through successive frozen stages, assuming the learned structure provides a benefit over purely local interactions.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the LP-QAOA circuit structure, showing the uncomputation/re-preparation cycle for the mixer, and comparison tables (e.g., Table 13) compare LP-QAOA against block-XY and standard QAOA variants on success probability and cost.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces LP-QAOA as a multistage protocol, proves a stability theorem for error bounding, and then validates its performance by comparing it against various QAOA baselines on structured optimization problems like BCST and SBM.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Many optimization problems reveal inexpensive structural information before requiring costly final evaluation, whereas the conventional quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applies a single aggregate objective throughout. We introduce the learned-projector quantum alternating operator ansatz (LP-QAOA), a multistage protocol that freezes optimized circuits and uses their output states to define later projector mixers. We prove a stability theorem for LP-QAOA that bounds the propagation of approximation errors through successive frozen stages. Our analysis also shows how learned-projector mixing avoids the high-order tunnelling suppression of local mixers. We conduct state-vector simulations on block-constrained spin tiling (BCST) instances, where LP-QAOA achieves higher probabilities of sampling the optimum, lower estimated logical-resource requirements, and better trainability than the tested baselines. A supporting stochastic block model experiment extends LP-QAOA to optimization problems with soft hierarchical structure. Our results highlight the potential of LP-QAOA to improve variational quantum optimization by exploiting hierarchical problem structure.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper investigates the local structure of vacuum entanglement in a free scalar field in Minkowski spacetime. It identifies specific 'Most Entangled Modes' (MEMs) that carry the majority of the distillable entanglement between two separated regions. By proposing a mode-swap protocol and analyzing convergence, the work pinpoints the exact field degrees of freedom responsible for accessible quantum correlations in QFT.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous quantification of vacuum entanglement structure using local field observables and the identification of specific 'entanglement carriers' (MEMs) provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding quantum correlations in QFT, which has implications for quantum information theory in curved or interacting backgrounds.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the fundamental question of which local field degrees of freedom in Quantum Field Theory (QFT) are responsible for encoding the accessible entanglement between two spatially separated regions in the vacuum.

**Main result.** The Most Entangled Modes (MEMs) are identified as the dominant carriers of distillable vacuum entanglement, and the entanglement measures (like Logarithmic Negativity) decay exponentially with separation distance.

**Method.** The authors employ the Klco-Beck-Savage method and propose a non-perturbative 'mode-swap entanglement harvesting protocol' to quantify entanglement using the covariance matrix and Logarithmic Negativity.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes a free massless real scalar field propagating in 1+3 Minkowski spacetime, focusing on entanglement between two disjoint spherical regions.

**Key observables.** Logarithmic Negativity (EN), Covariance Matrix ($\sigma$), Mutual Information ($I_{ab}$), and the spatial profiles of the MEMs (field and momentum smearing).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Separation distance ($d$), finite UV cutoff ($N$), and the dimensionality of spacetime (1+3 dimensions).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on restricting the field modes to a finite number $N$ (UV cutoff) and drawing analogies between 1+1 and 1+3 dimensions for convergence analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spatial profiles of the MEMs for various separations, and plots show the exponential decay of entanglement measures (EN, $I_{ab}$, $	ext{EF}$) with separation distance $d$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the problem of local entanglement structure, developing the MEM concept via the KBS method, quantifying entanglement using $	ext{EN}$, and finally analyzing the convergence properties of these modes in the continuum limit.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We find the shape of the modes containing most of the entanglement between two disjoint spherical regions in the vacuum of a free massless real scalar field in 1+3 Minkowski spacetime. Using the Klco-Beck-Savage method we approximate the field and momentum profile of the vacuum most entangled modes (MEMs) between two spheres. We define a non-perturbative mode-swap entanglement harvesting protocol where two spacelike separated probes extract the maximal amount of entanglement between two regions. Our results are a first step in the direction of understanding the local entanglement structure of quantum fields, pinpointing the exact degrees of freedom that encode accessible quantum correlations in QFT.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes quantum transport in disordered, one-dimensional chiral quantum systems near topological phase transitions. It proves that the quantum dynamics cause the position moments to grow logarithmically with time, mirroring classical Sinai diffusion. The analysis achieves this by relating the system's lowest energy eigenstate to the exponential of a random walk.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between quantum transport, localization phenomena, and classical diffusion models (Sinai) in the presence of disorder is highly relevant to understanding energy transport in disordered quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the quantum dynamics and transport properties at disorder-driven topological phase transitions in one-dimensional chiral quantum systems.

**Main result.** The quantum dynamics leads to a logarithmic growth of the moments of the position operator, similar to classical Sinai diffusion, providing a rigorous lower bound for this transport.

**Method.** The analysis uses spectral theory, approximating the lowest energy eigenfunction by the exponential of a random walk, and deriving lower bounds for time-averaged position moments.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by a random hopping Hamiltonian ($H_N$), which serves as a toy model for disorder-driven topological phase transitions in quasi-one-dimensional chiral Hamiltonians.

**Key observables.** Time- and disorder-averaged $q$-th moments of the position operator ($M_N^q(T)$), the smallest positive eigenvalue ($E_{N,1}$), and the eigenfunction components ($\phi_E$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The time scale $T$ is analyzed in a specific regime, $e^{c_1 N^\alpha} \le T \le e^{c_2 N^\alpha}$, and the system size $N$ is crucial.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on approximating the eigenstate by the exponential of a random walk and focusing on the diagonal terms in the moment expansion.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spatial profile of the smallest eigenvalue eigenfunction and associated random walks, and compare the distributions of the maximal eigenfunction values against zero-energy state predictions.

**Paper structure.** The work progresses by analyzing the spectral properties of the chiral Hamiltonian, establishing the relationship between the eigenstate and random walks, and finally deriving a rigorous lower bound for the position moments using these approximations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The random hopping Hamiltonian is a toy model for a disorder-driven topological phase transitions in one-dimensional chiral Hamiltonians. It has a vanishing Lyapunov exponent and a Dyson peak in the density of states at zero energy. This work shows how the quantum dynamics leads to a logarithmic growth of the moments of the position operator, similar as in classical Sinai diffusion. The mechanism at the origin of this phenomenon is that the eigenfunction of the smallest eigenvalue is well-approximated by the exponential of a classical random walk, leading to two essentially independent subexponential localization centers.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes using quantum optimization techniques to solve feature selection for complex biomedical data. It formulates the problem as minimizing a QUBO objective that balances feature importance and redundancy. The authors test this on quantum simulators and hardware, demonstrating feasibility while comparing performance against state-of-the-art classical methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the application is in biomedicine, the core methodology involves mapping a complex combinatorial optimization problem (feature selection) onto quantum hardware models (QUBO/Ising), which is a direct application of quantum computation theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of feature selection in high-dimensional biomedical data, specifically metabolomics, where the number of features vastly exceeds the number of samples.

**Main result.** The proposed QUBO formulation achieves competitive classification performance compared to classical methods and demonstrates hardware feasibility on NISQ devices, although it does not claim quantum advantage.

**Method.** The problem is formulated as minimizing a QUBO objective function that balances feature relevance (using Fisher score) against feature redundancy (using covariance). This optimization is solved using quantum algorithms like QAOA and BF-DCQO.

**Model / system.** The core model is the QUBO formulation, which is mapped onto an Ising cost Hamiltonian ($H_C$). This Hamiltonian is then solved using quantum optimization algorithms (QAOA, BF-DCQO) on a quantum gate-based computer.

**Key observables.** LOOCV accuracy across multiple classifiers (LDA, SVM, RF, etc.), circuit gate counts, and the convergence behavior of the quantum sampling distribution.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The balancing parameter $\alpha \in [0, 1]$, which weights the trade-off between feature relevance and redundancy.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results are limited by current NISQ hardware constraints and do not claim a quantum advantage; the QUBO formulation only accounts for quadratic interactions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the entire quantum feature selection pipeline from data input to quantum solver output. Figure 2 compares the gate counts required by BF-DCQO and QAOA for a 24-feature instance. Figure 7 shows the convergence of BF-DCQO sampling distribution over iterations.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for feature selection in metabolomics. It then details the novel QUBO formulation using Fisher scores and covariance. The methodology section describes mapping this to an Ising Hamiltonian and applying quantum solvers (QAOA, BF-DCQO) alongside classical baselines (ITS, filter/wrapper methods). Finally, results are presented comparing performance and feasibility.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Feature selection is an essential step for reducing complexity of high dimensional data, usually in preparation for developing machine learning models such as computational biomarkers. However, there are limitations associated with feature selection such as for metabolomic data where there are hundreds or even thousands of features per study participant, while the available number of participants in a clinical trials is limited. Classical methods such as exhaustive search require evaluation of all possible feature combinations, making them costly in terms of computation and runtime, or even infeasible, as feature dimensionality increases. In this study, we propose a novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) coefficient formulation and pose metabolomic feature selection as a QUBO problem that selects a specified number of features by balancing their relevance against redundancy among the selected variables. To evaluate our proposed QUBO objective function, we conducted a series of experiments using Bias-Field Digitized Counterdiabatic Quantum Optimization (BF-DCQO) and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on a quantum gate based computer. We also compared the method to several classical methods on three metabolomic datasets associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) on a classical computer. Our method reduces runtime compared with exhaustive search and Iterative Tabu Search (ITS) and achieves competitive performance across classifiers compared to classical filter, wrapper, and embedded methods. These results do not claim quantum advantage; rather, they establish hardware feasibility and demonstrate the current capabilities of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work demonstrates the ability to selectively control the ultrafast dynamics of coupled ferroelectric and magnetic orders in $	ext{BiFeO}_3$ by applying tensile strain. Using ultrafast electron diffraction, the researchers showed that strain specifically dampens the ferroelectric response without affecting the magnetic (AFD) response. This establishes strain as a powerful tool for engineering non-equilibrium phase control in correlated multiferroics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The selective control demonstrated here—tuning one order parameter while preserving another—is a key concept in designing quantum materials for advanced applications, relevant to understanding coupled dynamics in complex quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is achieving selective, non-equilibrium control over multiple coupled order parameters (like ferroelectric and magnetic) in quantum multiferroic materials.

**Main result.** Tensile strain selectively suppresses the ultrafast photoinduced dynamics associated with the ferroelectric order parameter, while leaving the dynamics related to the magnetic order parameter largely unaffected.

**Method.** The study uses *in situ* tensile strain tuning applied to freestanding $	ext{BiFeO}_3$ membranes, probed by MeV ultrafast electron diffraction following photoexcitation.

**Model / system.** The system is the multiferroic $	ext{BiFeO}_3$, which exhibits coupled ferroelectric (FE) and antiferrodistortive (AFD) orders. The experiment probes the ultrafast lattice dynamics associated with these two distinct order parameters.

**Key observables.** Photoinduced lattice dynamics, specifically the time evolution of FE displacement and AFD rotation, measured via changes in Bragg peak intensities ($\overline{I}_{	ext{odd}} - \overline{I}_{	ext{even}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Tunable uniaxial tensile strain ($\sim 0.2\%$), ultrafast time scales (sub-picosecond), and varying pump laser fluences.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis distinguishes between structural changes (FE/AFD reduction) and transient lattice heating (Debye-Waller effect).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the comparison of measured intensity changes against simple Debye-Waller scaling, and the time evolution of FE and AFD dynamics under varying strain and fluence.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the experimental platform, presents measurements showing the differential strain response of FE vs. AFD dynamics, and uses modeling (Ginzburg-Landau) to attribute the selective tuning to strain-mediated changes in carrier screening effects.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum materials are characterized by intertwined orders, and a fundamental goal in condensed matter physics is to achieve their selective control in such a way that one order parameter can be tuned while leaving others largely unaffected. Although significant progress has been made in thermal equilibrium, realizing such control out of equilibrium remains highly challenging. Here we employed \textit{in situ} tensile strain to selectively manipulate the photoinduced lattice dynamics associated with ferroelectric and magnetic orders in multiferroic BiFeO$_3$. By applying MeV ultrafast electron diffraction to freestanding BiFeO$_3$ membranes under tunable strain, we showed that tensile strain markedly suppresses the ultrafast photoinduced reduction of the ferroelectric displacement. By contrast, the photoinduced dynamics of the antiferrodistortive rotation of the oxygen octahedra, which modulates the magnetic order, remains insensitive to strain. Not only do these findings reveal distinct microscopic pathways underlying nonequilibrium multiferroic dynamics, they also establish tunable strain as an effective route for engineering ultrafast phase control in correlated materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This work precisely calculates the critical inverse temperature ($eta$) at which the Gibbs state of a Pauli Hamiltonian transitions from being separable (product state mixture) to entangled. The threshold, $z_\Delta$, depends universally on the maximum degree ($\Delta$) of the Hamiltonian's term-overlap graph. This provides a powerful tool for understanding thermal decoherence and entanglement decay in quantum many-body systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, quantitative threshold for when quantum correlations (entanglement) are expected to vanish in thermal equilibrium for local Hamiltonians, which is crucial for understanding quantum phase transitions in many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the exact universal high-temperature separability threshold for Gibbs states generated by Pauli Hamiltonians.

**Main result.** A sharp threshold $z_\Delta$ is established: the Gibbs state is separable if the inverse temperature $eta$ is below $z_\Delta$, and entangled otherwise.

**Method.** The proof uses inclusion-exclusion formulas and graph theory arguments applied to the term-overlap graph structure of the Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum many-body system governed by a Gibbs state $ho_eta(H) = e^{-eta H} / 	ext{Tr}(e^{-eta H})$, where $H$ is a Pauli Hamiltonian whose terms are constrained by a maximum overlap degree $\Delta$.

**Key observables.** Separability of the Gibbs state, the inverse temperature $eta$, and the threshold $z_\Delta$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The maximum degree $\Delta$ of the term-overlap graph, and the critical temperature $z_\Delta = 	ext{arctanh}\left[\max_{0\le x \le 1}x\left(rac{1-x}{1+x}ight)^{\Delta-1}ight]$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often focuses on the structure of the term-overlap graph, particularly when it is a tree, to derive the sharpest threshold.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the structure of a commuting tree Hamiltonian for specific parameters ($\Delta=3, b=2$), showing the relationship between terms and qubits on edges.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the threshold determination using decomposition techniques (inclusion-exclusion) to establish the separability criterion, followed by detailed analysis on the structure of the graph to find the critical temperature $z_\Delta$, and concludes with efficient sampling algorithms for the separable regime.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We determine the exact universal high-temperature separability threshold for Pauli Hamiltonians of bounded degree $Δ\ge2$. If every coefficient in the Hamiltonian has magnitude at most one and each term has overlapping support with at most $Δ$ other terms, the Gibbs state is a mixture of product Pauli eigenstates whenever \[   β\le z_Δ:= \operatorname{arctanh}\left[\max_{0\le x \le 1}x\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^{Δ-1} \right]. \] For every $β>z_Δ$, a finite commuting Hamiltonian with maximum overlap degree at most $Δ$ has an entangled Gibbs state. At any fixed $β<z_Δ$ strictly below the threshold, a classical polynomial-time algorithm produces samples from a distribution over product Pauli eigenstates approximating the Gibbs state in trace distance.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

This paper sets out a computational workflow that reconstructs the phylogeny of human Y-chromosome populations from a Variant Call Format (VCF) file of biallelic Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNP). The two classical phylogenetic decisions - topology selection and root placement - are cast as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation (QUBO) problems. The workflow combines two QUBO formulations with an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) decomposition strategy and a plug-in Digitized Counter-Diabatic Quantum Optimization (DCQO) solver, enabling large phylogenetic optimization problems to be executed across multiple classical or quantum computing resources. The DCQO gate-based optimizer drives each ADMM-block QUBO with short-depth counter-diabatic circuits in the impulse regime, without the necessity for an outer variational loop. The combination of ADMM decomposition and the DCQO block solver facilitates problem sizes that surpass the qubit budget of any individual digital quantum processing unit call, while maintaining the integrity of the original objective. The workflow extracts genotype information from VCF files, reconstructs topology and rooting through two QUBO formulations, and annotates the resulting tree using PhyloTree. The resultant data set comprises a Nexus-annotated rooted tree, in addition to diagnostic figures. The workflow demonstrates the potential of modest-scale QUBO formulations combined with ADMM decomposition to serve as a scalable alternative to greedy heuristics in the domain of population genomics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper resolves a major open problem in Boolean function complexity by proving that the approximate degree of block-composed functions composes multiplicatively. The authors establish the tight bound $\widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = \Theta(\widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g))$ using sophisticated tools from harmonic analysis and polynomial approximation theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the topic is in computational complexity theory, the use of polynomial approximation, spectral methods, and the connection to quantum query complexity makes it highly relevant to theoretical quantum information.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the open question of whether the approximate degree of block-composed Boolean functions composes multiplicatively.

**Main result.** It proves that for arbitrary total Boolean functions $f$ and $g$, the approximate degree satisfies $\widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = \Theta(\widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g))$.

**Method.** The proof involves establishing a matching lower bound by using advanced techniques involving trigonometric polynomials, squarefree extraction, and constructing specific probability measures derived from dual witnesses.

**Model / system.** The analysis is purely mathematical, focusing on the complexity measure known as the constant-error approximate degree ($\widetilde{deg}$) for total Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n	o\{0,1\}$ and $g:\{0,1\}^m	o\{0,1\}$.

**Key observables.** The approximate degree ($\widetilde{deg}$), the composition $f \circ g$, and the relationship $\widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = \Theta(\widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g))$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The approximation error $\epsilon$ (specifically $\epsilon=1/3$), the dimensions $n$ and $m$, and the degrees of the functions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the existence of an approximating polynomial $Q$ and the ability to control the frequency and structure of averaged functions $R$ derived from probability measures $ho_	heta$.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing upper bounds (known results) to tackling the lower bound. It develops tools using trigonometric polynomials and spectral decomposition to relate expectations over product distributions to expectations under specific, structured distributions ($
u(1+z)/2$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A longstanding open question in Boolean function complexity asks whether approximate degree composes multiplicatively under block composition. Although a general multiplicative upper bound is known, matching lower bounds have previously been established only for restricted classes of functions. We resolve this question for all total Boolean functions by proving the matching lower bound. Together with Sherstov's upper bound, our result shows that, for every pair of total Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ and $g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$, \[ \widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = Θ\!\left( \widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g) \right), \] where $\widetilde{deg}$ denotes constant-error approximate degree.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a rigorous connection between pseudoentanglement, a concept in quantum information theory, and the existence of cryptographic primitives called EFI pairs. By proving the equivalence between these concepts, the authors show that pseudoentanglement serves as a minimal, fundamental assumption for quantum cryptography. This bridges insights from quantum resource theory directly into the field of computational security.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a deep theoretical link between resource theories (entanglement) and computational complexity assumptions, which is foundational for understanding the limits of quantum cryptography.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental connection between the concept of pseudoentanglement and the necessary assumptions required for computational cryptography.

**Main result.** The existence of pseudoentanglement, under two different operational definitions, is shown to be a sufficient and necessary condition for the existence of EFI pairs, thereby bridging quantum information theory and cryptography.

**Method.** The authors establish mathematical relations between operational instances of pseudoentanglement and the hierarchy of minimal assumptions for computational cryptography, utilizing technical lemmas on entanglement measures and state distinguishability.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on quantum states, specifically families of states exhibiting pseudoentanglement, and the cryptographic primitive known as EFI pairs (efficiently preparable, statistically far, and computationally indistinguishable pairs).

**Key observables.** Computational entanglement measures, trace distance between state families, and the existence/non-existence of EFI pairs.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The security parameter $\lambda$, the error tolerance $\epsilon(\lambda)$, and the entanglement gap bounds $c(\lambda)$ and $d(\lambda)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The underlying state families for pseudoentanglement are assumed to be efficiently preparable for the cryptographic constructions to hold.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 conceptually maps physical worlds (entanglement, AdS/CFT) to computational cryptography worlds via the relationship between pseudoentanglement and EFI pairs. Figure 2 details the implications, such as Fully-computational pseudoentanglement $\implies$ EFI pairs.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the connection by first establishing the sufficiency of pseudoentanglement for EFI pairs using different operational definitions, and then proving the equivalence between these definitions and the existence of EFI pairs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The advent of pseudoentanglement and computational entanglement theory bootstrapped a wave of research at the intersection of computer science and information theory. In parallel, computational cryptography has undergone substantial development, prompted by the introduction of pseudorandom states and followed by the establishment of a baseline for the computational hardness required for quantum cryptography, from which EFI pairs emerge as a central primitive. We study the connection between pseudoentanglement and computational cryptography through EFI pairs. Our goal is to enable the use of resources arising from computational entanglement theory in the field of cryptography. For this, we establish the relation between operational instances of pseudoentanglement and the hierarchy of minimal assumptions for computational cryptography. We show that the existence of pseudoentanglement under two different operational definitions, with efficient state generation, is a sufficient condition for the existence of EFI pairs. Combined with a previously established result that the converse also holds under the second definition, this allows us to also demonstrate their equivalence. This places pseudoentanglement alongside other minimal assumptions in cryptography, not only offering an alternative perspective on this fundamental problem, but also building a bridge that allows insights from either area to inform the other. While proving these theorems, we introduce and demonstrate technical lemmas in quantum information and computational entanglement theory, relating the computational entanglement measures to the distance between states, establishing distinguishing conditions for mixtures of two families given pairwise distances between their states, and demonstrating the first continuity relation for a computational entanglement measure.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously proves that the regularized Rényi divergence of quantum channels converges to the regularized relative entropy as the Rényi order approaches one. By establishing this continuity, the authors derive powerful results concerning quantum hypothesis testing, including sharp zero-one laws and asymptotic equipartition properties for quantum channels.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental mathematical tools for quantifying distinguishability between quantum processes (channels), which is crucial for understanding channel capacity and the limits of quantum communication protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper proves the continuity of the regularized, stabilized sandwiched Rényi divergence of quantum channels as the Rényi order approaches one.

**Main result.** The limit of the regularized Rényi divergence equals the regularized relative entropy, and this result yields strong converses for quantum hypothesis testing and channel discrimination.

**Method.** The proof utilizes advanced tools from quantum information theory, including Stinespring decompositions, Schatten norm estimates, and asymptotic analysis of block-encoded testing bounds.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on finite-dimensional quantum channels, $N$ and $M$, mapping between the spaces of linear operators $\mathcal{L}(A) 	o \mathcal{L}(B)$. The context is quantum hypothesis testing and channel capacity.

**Key observables.** Regularized Rényi Divergence ($D_{	ext{reg}}^\alpha(N\|M)$), Regularized Relative Entropy ($D_{	ext{reg}}(N\|M)$), and quantum hypothesis testing error bounds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rényi order $\alpha$, block length $n$, and the max-relative entropy $d_\infty$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes finite-dimensional spaces and relies on the existence of Stinespring isometries for the core proofs.

**Figures summary.** No specific figures are described, but the text references mathematical theorems and lemmas (e.g., Lemma 2, Lemma 3) that build the proof structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the continuity theorem (Theorem 1) by relating the Rényi divergence to the relative entropy. It then uses this result to derive strong converses for channel discrimination and proves the Subchannel Asymptotic Equipartition Property (Corollary 6) and the sharp zero-one law (Corollary 8).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove that the regularized, stabilized sandwiched Rényi divergence of finite-dimensional quantum channels converges to their regularized relative entropy as the Rényi order tends to one. The key tool is the channel hockey-stick divergence: Gour's Stinespring approximation bound and a Schatten norm estimate amplify an asymptotic bound below one into exponential decay at higher threshold rates. For channel pairs with finite max-relative entropy, known operational connections then give exponential strong converses for parallel and adaptive discrimination, a sharp zero--one testing law, and the subchannel asymptotic equipartition property.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on abstract quantum codes, the rigorous mathematical framework for optimizing resource trade-offs (rate vs. distance) is highly relevant to designing physical quantum hardware architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge addressed is reducing the qubit overhead in quantum error correction (QEC) to achieve scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

**Main result.** The authors developed systematic design principles and templates to explore the trade-offs among encoding rate, distance, and check weight, identifying numerous compact, high-performing quantum codes.

**Method.** The work involves developing systematic design heuristics, analyzing code templates (like pair-partition constructions), and employing advanced techniques such as ensemble analysis and density evolution to estimate performance thresholds.

**Model / system.** The focus is on designing and analyzing ultra-high-rate quantum codes, specifically low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, which are characterized by parameters like blocklength, distance, and encoding rate.

**Key observables.** Encoding rate, distance (d), check weight, blocklength (n), and the residual error probability threshold.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical error rates (e.g., 0.1%), degree distributions (row/column weight), and the design parameters $(J, L)$ for specific code families.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on developing systematic frameworks to navigate the design space and uses ensemble estimates, which are noted to be heuristic screens rather than definitive proofs of the logical distance.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate design heuristics, pairing graphs for code construction, and comparisons of Pareto frontiers between certified bounds and ensemble estimates.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Reducing the qubit overhead of quantum error correction is a central challenge for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Recent ultra-high-rate quantum codes offer a promising route toward this goal, with some constructions requiring as few as two physical data qubits per logical qubit. However, systematic principles for navigating the tradeoffs among encoding rate, distance, check weight, and blocklength remain lacking. Here, we develop and analyze principles for exploring this design space, and use them to design compact code constructions with improved performance. We develop code templates based on a pair-partition construction and a halving transformation that further reduces blocklength. Motivated by ensemble analysis of the degree distributions, we identify column weight as a key design parameter: increasing the column weight enables larger distances at compact blocklengths, at the cost of heavier checks. We find that at physical error rates of 0.1%, the benefits of increased distance often outweigh the penalty associated with heavier checks. Applying this framework, we identify numerous compact codes with favorable parameters, including [[90,21,11]], [[140,31,15]], and [[200,43,20]] non-CSS codes with check weight 10. Moreover, we develop symmetry-informed strategies for identifying low-weight logical bases. These results provide systematic strategies for designing ultra-high-rate quantum codes and navigating their Pareto frontier.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an efficient method to synthesize Multi-Controlled Toffoli gates using a ternary qutrit system. By employing a hierarchical, tree-based decomposition, it reduces the circuit depth from linear to logarithmic scaling for balanced control widths. This offers a practical, resource-efficient building block for advanced fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on quantum computation, the resource optimization techniques (depth reduction, ancillary qubit minimization) are highly relevant to designing efficient quantum circuits for physical platforms like trapped ions or superconducting qubits where gate depth and ancillary overhead are primary limitations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently synthesizing Multi-Controlled Toffoli (MCT) gates, which are crucial primitives for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

**Main result.** A novel intermediate-qutrit decomposition achieves logarithmic depth scaling ($\Theta(\log n)$) for balanced control widths, significantly outperforming linear-depth recursive baselines.

**Method.** The authors propose a hierarchical, tree-based decomposition strategy utilizing temporary occupation of a third qutrit level to evaluate multi-controlled logic.

**Model / system.** The work is set in a ternary qutrit model ($\mathcal{H}_3$) where the computation logic is confined to a binary subspace, using the third level as a temporary workspace state.

**Key observables.** Logical P9 injection count ($6n+3$), clean ancillary qutrit count ($n-3/4$), and circuit depth ($\Theta(\log n)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Control width ($n$), balanced core width ($m=2^h-1$), and the underlying resource model (ternary Clifford+P9).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The decomposition relies on the temporary occupation of the qutrit level $|2angle$, and comparisons are made within the specific ternary Clifford+P9 resource model.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the overall decomposition structure, detailing the forward tree computation (leaf blocks, internal merges, root toggle) and the inverse traversal for state restoration.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the tree computation via leaf and internal merge blocks, analyzes the resource costs for balanced widths ($n=2h-1$), and then extends the construction to arbitrary widths by appending sequential controls, comparing results against established recursive baselines.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Temporary occupation of qutrit levels can reduce the width and depth required for binary circuit logic in quantum computing. We introduce an efficient intermediate-qutrit decomposition of multi-controlled Toffoli gates with binary-subspace inputs and outputs. For balanced control widths $n=2^h-1$, the proposed decomposition is evaluated hierarchically through a tree, allowing independent subtree computations to proceed in parallel and reducing the depth from linear to logarithmic. The balanced low-depth construction requires $6n+3$ logical $P_9$ injections and $\frac{n-3}{4}$ clean ancillary qutrits. It matches the direct $P_9$ count of a recursively extended Clifford+$P_9$ baseline derived from the state-of-the-art work while using asymptotically one-quarter as many clean ancillas and replacing linear depth with logarithmic depth. For arbitrary control widths, a sequential extension preserves the $6n+3$ $P_9$ count but has depth $O(\log m+n-m)$ for a balanced core $m=2^h-1\leq n$, which is linear in the worst case over $n$. By reducing the resource overhead of a widely used reversible primitive, the proposed decomposition provides a practical building block for the design and compilation of more resource-efficient quantum algorithms in the fault-tolerant regime.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously tests how the sequence in which quantum circuit optimization passes are applied affects the final circuit quality. By systematically testing permutations, the authors prove that the order matters, leading to the proposal of a recommended, optimized sequence. This work is vital for compiler developers aiming to minimize noise and resource usage on real quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on compilation rather than physical dynamics, understanding the systematic limitations and dependencies within quantum hardware toolchains is crucial for designing algorithms that are robust to compiler choices, which is a key concern in quantum information theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the critical, yet largely unexplored, issue of how the order of optimization passes affects the final quality of quantum circuit compilation.

**Main result.** The order of optimization passes significantly impacts circuit quality, demonstrating clear dependencies between passes, although the best order depends heavily on the native gate set and surrounding compiler passes.

**Method.** The authors systematically evaluated pairwise and multi-pass combinations of 16 optimization passes using Qiskit, measuring circuit depth and gate count across various benchmark circuits.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on optimizing abstract quantum circuits intended for execution on near-term quantum hardware, using established quantum compilation toolchains.

**Key observables.** Circuit depth and gate count (measured via metrics like R_m(p)).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The set of 16 optimization passes, the target native gate set (e.g., IBM Falcon, IonQ Forte), and the specific benchmark circuit used.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis initially focuses on passes before hardware mapping, and the results are derived from testing specific, limited combinations of passes.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the sequential phases of quantum circuit compilation. Figure 6 compares performance metrics (Depth, Gate Count) between Qiskit's default order and the paper's recommended order.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the problem (order dependence) to systematic testing of pairwise combinations, analyzing correction mechanisms via repetition, and finally proposing a recommended, structured sequence based on pass classes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum circuit optimization is critical for mitigating the noise inherent in current quantum hardware. Quantum compilers typically sequentially apply multiple optimizations (also called ``optimization passes'') to improve the circuit. The impact of the order in which these passes are executed has yet been largely unexplored. This paper investigates the significance of the order of optimization passes within quantum circuit compilation, specifically analyzing interactions between different optimization methods and quantifying their mutual influences. Using Qiskit's compiler, we systematically evaluate pairwise combinations of 16 selected optimization passes, measuring circuit depth and gate count across various benchmark circuits. Our findings indicate dependencies between certain optimization passes, demonstrating that the order of the passes affects the optimization quality. In some cases, the worse performing sequence can be corrected through repeated pass application. %such that they are as good as the best performing one by extending the sequence. Experiments on multi-pass sequences show that more than two optimization passes may have an impact on each other but that this always links to the previously found pairwise effects. We observe that it is important to initially choose the best order of optimization passes to get the best possible optimization for the given circuit. The experiments reveal some factors which are important to choose the best, or at least a good, order; among those, the resulting optimization sequence depends the most on the native gate set.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces ZX-QAS, a novel, evaluation-efficient framework for Quantum Architecture Search designed for noisy quantum devices. It mitigates high computational costs by integrating ZX-calculus topological reuse with a Gray-code mapping to manage the search space. The approach successfully demonstrates stable convergence and significant cost reduction for simulating quantum many-body systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical limitations of applying quantum algorithms to near-term hardware by providing a computationally efficient method to explore the vast space of quantum circuits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) for Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQA) suffers from prohibitively high evaluation costs due to the need for repeated training and evaluation of many candidate circuits.

**Main result.** The proposed ZX-QAS framework significantly reduces the cost of expensive evaluations under noisy conditions while maintaining stable convergence for tasks like ground-state energy estimation.

**Method.** The framework combines a noise-aware quantum neural network with a ZX-calculus topological reuse mechanism and uses a ternary Gray-code mapping to implicitly encode the search space.

**Model / system.** The work targets NISQ devices applied to quantum chemistry and many-body physics, exemplified by the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. The search space is managed using ZX-calculus graphs and a Gray-code mapping.

**Key observables.** Ground-state energy estimation, stable convergence, and the reduction in the number of required circuit evaluations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise parameters (e.g., $p_{BF}$ for bit-flip, $T_1, T_2$ for relaxation), the similarity threshold for topological reuse, and the number of qubits ($N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that structural similarity, quantifiable via ZX-calculus, can serve as an effective prior to reuse computational results and reduce the evaluation budget.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the basic graphical elements and rewrite rules of ZX-calculus, and a workflow diagram shows the three steps of the ZX-QAS framework: mapping, training, and reuse.

**Paper structure.** The paper first identifies the high cost of QAS, then introduces the ZX-QAS framework which uses a ternary Gray-code mapping for efficient search space encoding. It details the noise-aware training using supernets and finally leverages the ZX-calculus for topological reuse during the search process.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Variational quantum algorithm is a leading approach for quantum chemistry and many-body physics on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The performance depends strongly on the structure of the parameterized quantum circuits. Quantum architecture search (QAS) can automate ansatz design. However, it requires repeated training and evaluation of many candidate circuits, leading to high evaluation cost. In this work, we propose a noise-aware quantum architecture search framework based on ZX-calculus topological reuse (ZX-QAS). The framework encodes the search space with a ternary Gray-code mapping and integrates a noise-aware quantum neural network with a ZX-calculus topological reuse mechanism. The effectiveness of the framework is validated through ground-state energy estimation tasks and one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model tasks under noisy conditions. The results show that the ZX-QAS exhibits stable convergence and remarkably reduces the cost of expensive evaluations under noisy conditions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses transport and thermodynamic measurements on UTe2 under pressure to map out its complex phase diagram. It identifies a hidden antiferromagnetic order existing within the superconducting dome. The key finding is that this magnetic order vanishes at the same point where the material enters a bulk 3D antiferromagnetic phase, suggesting this hidden magnetism drives the unconventional superconductivity via a quantum critical point.

**Why it may be interesting.** The strong interplay between magnetic fluctuations (AFM/FM) and unconventional superconductivity in a heavy-fermion material like UTe2 provides a rich platform for studying quantum critical points and pairing mechanisms relevant to strongly correlated electron systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the nature of the magnetism responsible for unconventional superconductivity in UTe2, specifically focusing on hidden magnetic order within the superconducting dome.

**Main result.** The measurements reveal a hidden antiferromagnetic order that vanishes concurrently with superconductivity when a high-pressure 3D antiferromagnetic phase is induced, suggesting a quantum critical point drives the pairing.

**Method.** The study utilizes AC magnetic susceptibility and AC heat capacity measurements under applied pressure and magnetic fields to map out the phase diagram.

**Model / system.** The physical system is UTe2, a heavy-fermion superconductor, whose superconducting dome is tuned by external pressure and magnetic fields to reveal competing magnetic phases.

**Key observables.** Superconducting critical temperature (Tc), magnetic susceptibility ($\chi(T)$), heat capacity ($C/T$), and the presence/disappearance of Hidden Magnetic Order (HMO) and 3D Antiferromagnetic (AFM) transitions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Applied pressure (up to 1.5 GPa) and magnetic field strength (up to 7 T).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The hidden magnetic order is assumed to be antiferromagnetic in nature, and its critical point is hypothesized to coincide with the maximum Tc of the superconducting dome.

**Figures summary.** Figures show magnetic susceptibility confirming the HMO transition within the SC2 dome, heat capacity confirming the HMO anomaly, and phase diagrams illustrating the competition between SC2, HMO, and the 3D-AFM phase under varying P and H.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically measures magnetic and thermodynamic properties across a phase diagram, identifying the HMO within the SC2 dome, correlating its disappearance with the onset of the 3D-AFM phase, and extrapolating to a QCP at the maximum Tc.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Unconventional superconductivity typically occurs near magnetic instabilities, and the corresponding spin fluctuations are widely believed to play a crucial role in mediating electron pairing. UTe$_2$ is a promising candidate for exhibiting multiple spin-triplet superconducting phases when tuning with applied pressure and magnetic fields, but the nature of the magnetism driving these unconventional pairing states is undetermined. Our measurements of UTe$_2$ under applied pressures and magnetic fields reveal the presence of a magnetic order hidden within the pressure-induced superconducting dome, which vanishes together with the superconductivity once there is sufficiently high pressure to induce the three-dimensional antiferromagnetic phase. Extrapolation of the phase boundary of the hidden magnetic order, which is most likely antiferromagnetic in nature, points to a zero-temperature quantum critical point that coincides with the maximum transition temperature of the pressure-induced superconducting dome, suggesting that it could corresponds to the parent magnetic phase of the critical antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations driving the triplet superconductivity. These findings advance the understanding of the interplay of magnetism and superconductivity in an exemplar candidate triplet superconductor, which is necessary for revealing the microscopic origin of the different unconventional superconducting phases.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops and tests reinforcement learning policies to optimally schedule simultaneous entanglement requests in quantum networks. By framing the problem as an MDP solved with DQN and MPNNs, the authors demonstrate that their learned policies robustly manage resource constraints better than existing heuristics. The paper also introduces a novel method using LLMs to extract interpretable policies from the trained model.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on optimizing resource scheduling and managing complex, time-dependent quantum resources (entanglement) is highly relevant to the practical implementation of quantum networking protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of finding an optimal policy to schedule multiple, simultaneous entanglement requests (experiments) in a quantum network while minimizing resource usage and latency.

**Main result.** The learned reinforcement learning policies significantly outperform baseline heuristics, maintaining high success rates even when the physical link activation probability is substantially lower than the baseline.

**Method.** The problem is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and solved using Double Deep Q-Networks (DQN) combined with Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs).

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum network modeled as a multi-graph where tasks require generating virtual links via entanglement swapping over physical links with age and decoherence constraints.

**Key observables.** Success rate (%), Mean Step Count, and the ability to maintain performance under varying link activation probabilities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Link activation probability ($p_l$), experiment duration ($d_k$), and the network topology (e.g., starlink, grid).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumes entanglement swapping succeeds deterministically, and the LLM heuristic extraction is a promising method for interpreting complex learned policies.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the success rate and mean step count of various heuristics against the learned policy across different network topologies and noise levels.

**Paper structure.** The paper first formulates the scheduling problem as an MDP, then applies DQN/MPNNs with curriculum training. It details performance comparisons against heuristics, and finally explores methods for policy interpretation using LLMs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Future quantum networks will make use of entanglement to perform numerous tasks, such as sending quantum information over long distances, distributed quantum computing, and quantum sensing. In general, these tasks will need to be performed simultaneously in various regions of a network, while minimizing resources and latency. We will thus require policies for scheduling link-level entanglement resources, and using the link-level entanglement to create various forms of multipartite entanglement required for every task. In this work, we address this problem using reinforcement learning. We formulate a Markov Decision Process for the problem and use double deep Q-networks (DQN) with Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), experience replay buffers, and curriculum training to obtain policies. The key physical parameter is the probability of link-level entanglement generation, i.e., the link activation probability. We show that our policies maintain 100% success for up to 71% lower link activation probability than the baseline heuristics for a set of physically relevant network topologies. We then examine an additional constraint where experiment (task) placements are restricted to specific hardware types and demonstrate a similar advantage in performance over heuristics, with our policy maintaining at least an 80% success rate for up to a 59% lower link activation probability. Finally, we explore methods to interpret the learned policy by defining metrics enabling conclusions to be drawn about the model's behavior and by tasking a large language model (LLM) to derive a novel heuristic given example actions taken by the DQN-trained policy. We find that the LLM heuristic performs similarly to the DQN-trained policy in performance, indicating a promising method for interpretable policy extraction for large quantum networks, where direct training becomes computationally expensive.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work establishes a microscopic mechanism for the emergence of Majorana zero modes in PDW superconductors. By analyzing the energy cost of vortex splitting, the authors predict a field-induced transition to a half-vortex lattice. This lattice structure is then modeled using an effective Majorana Hamiltonian, revealing characteristic nodal or line-crossing features in the resulting electronic band structure.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit derivation of a microscopic route from a superconducting state (PDW) to a topological superconducting state (Majorana lattice) via vortex physics is highly relevant for understanding emergent topological phases in condensed matter systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the energetic stabilization of half-quantum vortices, which are theorized to bind Majorana zero modes, within Pair-Density-Wave (PDW) superconductors.

**Main result.** The analysis shows that the core energy gain favors the splitting of full vortices into half-vortices, leading to a field-induced transition and the formation of a Majorana lattice with characteristic Dirac nodes or Fermi lines.

**Method.** The study employs Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculations to determine stiffnesses and Ginzburg-Landau couplings, followed by constructing and diagonalizing an effective Majorana hopping Hamiltonian in momentum space.

**Model / system.** The system is a spinless honeycomb-lattice model exhibiting a PDW phase. The physics is governed by the competition between long-range logarithmic vortex interactions and short-range core energy contributions derived from the Ginzburg-Landau potential.

**Key observables.** Superfluid stiffness ($ho$), PDW relative-phase stiffness ($\kappa$), vortex energy difference ($\Delta E$), and the energy spectrum $E_{\pm}(k)$ of the Majorana Hamiltonian.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The stiffness ratio $\kappa/ho$, the critical magnetic field $B_c$, and the hopping-sign sector $\eta = \pm 1$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The long-range physics is dominated by logarithmic interactions, but the final equilibrium separation is dictated by the core energy stabilization mechanism.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing the full-to-half-vortex transition and the Majorana band structure, which exhibits isolated Dirac nodes for certain parameters ($\eta=-1, d=1/2$) and direct band-touching loci for others ($\eta=1, d=1/2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the PDW phase and calculating stiffnesses ($ho, \kappa$), to determining the field-driven vortex fractionalization via core energy analysis, and finally constructing and analyzing the resulting effective Majorana lattice Hamiltonian in momentum space.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Pair-density-wave (PDW) superconductors admit half-quantum vortices that can bind Majorana zero modes, but whether such defects are energetically stabilized in microscopic models remains unclear. We address this question in a spinless honeycomb-lattice model with a PDW phase. Microscopic Hartree-Fock calculations determine the superfluid stiffness $ρ$ and PDW relative-phase stiffness $κ$, and show that $κ/ρ$ approaches unity near the continuous PDW--Dirac-semimetal transition, strongly reducing the long-wavelength cost of vortex fractionalization. Combining this with microscopically extracted Ginzburg--Landau couplings, we show that vortex-core energetics favor fractionalization, producing a strongly enhanced splitting scale and a field-driven full-vortex--to--half-vortex lattice transition. We determine the resulting two-flavor half-vortex lattice structure and construct the associated Majorana lattice. Majorana hybridization produces geometry- and flux-dependent bands with Dirac nodes and zero-energy Fermi lines. Together, these results establish a microscopic route from PDW superconductivity to field-induced half-vortex and Majorana lattices.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a molecular theory to explain the universal two-branch Baumgärtel-Schausberger-Winter relaxation spectrum found in polymer melts. By independently calculating contributions from segmental motion and contour-length fluctuations, the authors predict the characteristic $	au^{-2/3} + 	au^{1/4}$ form. This provides a fundamental, non-empirical understanding of how different microscopic processes contribute to the overall viscoelastic response of disordered materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a rigorous theoretical framework connecting microscopic dynamics (segmental motion, path fluctuations) to macroscopic viscoelastic signatures (BSW spectrum), which is a key goal in understanding complex many-body dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To derive a molecular origin for the robust two-branch Baumgärtel-Schausberger-Winter (BSW) relaxation spectrum observed in entangled polymer melts and related disordered systems.

**Main result.** The theory successfully predicts the BSW form ($	ext{H}_s(	au) \propto 	au^{-2/3} + 	au^{1/4}$) by showing a continuous transfer of stress relaxation between two independently derived molecular dynamics sectors.

**Method.** The authors constructed a molecular theory analyzing chain segment motion relative to a screened environment, combining Gaussian-chain preaveraging with longitudinal primitive-path diffusion calculations.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on entangled polymer melts and particle rafts, modeling the dynamics using a coarse-grained description involving two coupled dynamic sectors: fast segmental motion and slower cage/constraint field evolution.

**Key observables.** The BSW spectrum ($	ext{G}'(\omega)$ and $	ext{G}''(\omega)$), characterized by two distinct algebraic relaxation cascades joined by a smooth minimum.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The exponents characterizing the two sectors: $	au^{-2/3}$ (cooperative) and $	au^{1/4}$ (longitudinal/CLF).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory assumes that the BSW spectrum arises from the coupling of two distinct dynamical sectors, and it tests the derived operator against experimental data without fitting spectral exponents.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the molecular-weight-constrained fit of $	ext{G}'$ and $	ext{G}''$ for PBD melts, showing common molecular-weight laws, and map the predicted $(1/4, 2/3)$ exponent point on existing BSW sets.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the empirical BSW spectrum, develops a molecular theory based on segment motion relative to a cage, derives two independent power-law behaviors ($	au^{-2/3}$ and $	au^{1/4}$), and finally tests the combination against experimental polymer melt data.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Entangled polymer melts exhibit the robust two-branch Baumgärtel-Schausberger-Winter (BSW) relaxation spectrum, while related spectra occur in nonpolymeric monodisperse disordered systems. In spite of the successful application of BSW to many different materials, a molecular derivation of these spectra is lacking. We construct a molecular theory in which a chain segment moves relative to a screened, dynamically responding multichain environment. Gaussian-chain preaveraging gives $M_{\rm seg}(Δm)\sim(Δm)^{-1/2}$, hence $λ_p\sim p^{3/2}$ and, after stress projection, $H(τ)\simτ^{-2/3}$. Independently, longitudinal primitive-path diffusion gives contour-length fluctuations with $H(τ)\simτ^{1/4}$. A molecular-weight-constrained implementation is tested simultaneously against experimental $G'(ω)$ and $G''(ω)$ data for four monodisperse polybutadiene (PBD) melts, without fitting spectral exponents or individual modal weights. The resulting BSW spectrum exhibits a continuous transfer from the fast cooperative to the slow constraint-renewal cascade before a finite-chain terminal edge. A common two-sector caged dynamics then connects polymers to particle rafts without assuming identical microscopic mechanisms.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces MQSS-Selector, a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to solve the complex problem of quantum program compilation. It unifies device selection and compiler pass optimization into a single scheduler to maximize performance metrics like fidelity and minimize latency. This is crucial for bridging classical HPC resources with error-prone quantum hardware in the NISQ era.

**Why it may be interesting.** It addresses the critical software stack challenges in realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation by providing a learning-based optimization layer for resource-constrained NISQ devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge of optimizing quantum program compilation by jointly selecting the best quantum device and the optimal sequence of compiler optimization passes.

**Main result.** The authors propose MQSS-Selector, an RL-guided framework that unifies device selection and pass ordering to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously.

**Method.** They leverage Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents interacting with a simulated quantum software stack environment to learn optimal scheduling policies.

**Model / system.** The system targets High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) infrastructures operating in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, dealing with quantum circuits and compilation pipelines.

**Key observables.** Fidelity (Hellinger fidelity), compilation time, scheduling latency, program depth, and operation count.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Device topology, gate fidelity, queueing delay, and the set of available compiler passes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The joint optimization problem is shown to be NP-hard, necessitating heuristic/approximation algorithms like RL.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the integrated scheduling pipeline combining device selection and phase ordering optimization for quantum program execution.

**Paper structure.** The paper frames the problem as a Design Space Exploration (DSE) and proposes a unified RL selector, detailing components for device selection (using supervised ML) and pass ordering (using RL).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

High Performance Computing (HPC) and Quantum Computing (QC) systems are increasingly converging towards unified High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) infrastructures, driven by a growing need to bridge classical and quantum workflows, which affects all levels of the system stack, from the hardware to compilers and runtimes, all the way to applications. However, today's QC devices are still in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, are error-prone and resource-limited, and therefore require specialized optimizations and topology mappings to achieve sufficient fidelity. This places special emphasis on proper compilation and optimization within the overall quantum software stack. Many existing stacks remain fragmented, with separate components responsible for device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and job queue scheduling. This paper proposes a unified, learning-based selector that integrates these disparate stages into a cohesive framework. Our proposed selector scheme leverages reinforcement learning and deep learning models that can be extended to simultaneously optimize multiple objectives -- such as fidelity, compilation time, and scheduling latency -- while dynamically adapting to circuit characteristics and device conditions.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a general framework for constructing advanced non-Abelian quantum LDPC codes by utilizing sheaf theory and cup products. It achieves codes with desirable parameters like constant rate and linear distance, extending error correction beyond standard Pauli stabilizers. These results offer a concrete theoretical tool for investigating non-Abelian topological phases and magic state generation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The extension of quantum error correction theory into non-Abelian structures and the connection to topological phases of matter is highly relevant for understanding robust quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing and analyzing non-Abelian quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes to extend quantum error correction beyond the limitations of traditional Pauli stabilizer codes.

**Main result.** The authors constructed non-Abelian qLDPC codes with constant encoding rate and linear distance by gauging sheaf codes via cup products, providing a foundation for exploring non-Abelian phases.

**Method.** The work employs advanced mathematical tools from algebraic topology, specifically gauging sheaf codes using cup products within a framework of cochain complexes.

**Model / system.** The model involves non-Abelian quantum codes, which connect quantum error correction, phases of matter, and computational resources. The construction is based on generalizing sheaf codes using cell complexes.

**Key observables.** Code distance (characterized by the general Knill–Laflamme condition), encoding rate, and the presence of 'long-range magic' throughout the code space.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Constant encoding rate and linear distance ($	ext{[[N} \Theta(N), \Theta(N)]]$); the structure of the underlying cell complex $X$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis requires moving beyond the traditional Pauli stabilizer setting and carefully handling logical constraints in the gauged code space.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the general problem, develops the mathematical framework using sheaf theory and cup products, constructs the qLDPC codes, and analyzes their properties like distance and magic state preparation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Non-Abelian quantum codes connect quantum error correction, phases of matter, and computational resources. In this work, we develop a general framework for constructing non-Abelian quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes by gauging sheaf codes via cup products and use it to obtain families with constant encoding rate and linear distance. We resolve the coupled logical constraints using explicit representatives to characterize the full gauged code space. We provide a fundamental treatment of code distance based on the general Knill--Laflamme condition and combine expansion with cleaning to establish protection against arbitrary low-weight errors. We further construct an almost-good family whose entire code space exhibits long-range magic. Gauging and ungauging also enable logical Clifford measurements that prepare encoded magic states. These results extend good qLDPC codes beyond the Pauli stabilizer setting and provide a concrete foundation for exploring non-Abelian phases beyond geometric locality and pursuing the no low-energy trivial magic conjecture.

</details>
