**Summary.** This work analyzes the theoretical link between quantum generative models and the hardness of sampling from unknown data sources. It proves that transferring sampling hardness requires solving a difficult distribution certification problem, which demands exponentially many samples. Consequently, practitioners cannot generally assume that polynomial sampling efforts are enough to justify claiming source-level sampling hardness.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous theoretical constraint on the claims made in quantum machine learning, showing that simply training a quantum model does not guarantee that the unknown data source possesses the desirable computational hardness property.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the sampling hardness property of a quantum generative model can be reliably transferred to an unknown, real-world data-generating distribution when trained on finite classical samples.

**Main result.** Transferring sampling hardness requires certifying a global relationship between the two distributions, which necessitates an exponentially large number of samples for high-entropy distributions, meaning polynomial samples are generally insufficient.

**Method.** The authors reduce the hardness transfer problem to a distribution certification problem, utilizing existing lower bounds from identity testing and total-variation distance analysis.

**Model / system.** The focus is on Quantum Generative Models (QGMs) based on quantum circuit families, comparing the inherent hardness of the generator itself (generator-level hardness) versus the hardness of the unknown source distribution (source-level hardness).

**Key observables.** Total-Variation Distance ($d_{TV}$), Sample Requirement ($m$), Min-Entropy ($h$), and the $\ell_1$-distance threshold ($ho$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The required sample complexity is shown to scale exponentially with the entropy of the distribution, and the analysis distinguishes between the complexity of the known-target certification problem and statistical fitting.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the most favorable certification setting (known target distribution, unlimited computational power) and relies on established lower bounds for identity testing.

**Figures summary.** Not specified.

**Paper structure.** The paper first distinguishes between generator-level and source-level hardness, then establishes that transferring hardness requires solving a distribution certification problem, which is then bounded by known lower bounds derived from identity testing.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum generative models are often motivated by circuit families whose output distributions are believed to be classically hard to sample from. When such models are trained on ordinary classical datasets, however, this hardness does not automatically transfer to the unknown data-generating distribution. We show that transferring sampling hardness via total-variation closeness from a quantum model to an unknown source requires certifying a global relation between the two distributions, thereby reducing the problem to distribution certification. Combining this reduction with existing certification lower bounds yields an exponential sample requirement for the high-entropy distributions relevant to many sampling-hardness proposals. Consequently, polynomially many samples cannot, in general, justify attributing sampling hardness to an unknown data-generating distribution. Moreover, even classically trivial distributions, such as the uniform distribution and product distributions, require exponentially many samples to certify in the absence of structural assumptions. Our results clarify the role of sampling hardness in quantum generative modeling and distinguish generator-level hardness from source-level hardness when learning from ordinary datasets.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenging one-shot routing problem in quantum networks, where the goal is maximizing connection fidelity from finite resources. The authors develop the FOLD heuristic, a polynomial-time algorithm that efficiently finds near-optimal routing schedules by intelligently interleaving entanglement swapping and distillation. This work is vital for designing scalable quantum communication protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, computationally tractable algorithm (FOLD) for optimizing resource utilization in quantum communication networks, which is crucial for scaling up quantum internet infrastructure.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the complex 'one-shot routing' problem in quantum networks, which requires optimizing end-to-end fidelity from a fixed, limited set of entangled resources rather than maximizing the rate of resource generation.

**Main result.** The proposed heuristic, FOLD, runs in polynomial time and achieves near-optimal end-to-end fidelity, significantly outperforming exact scheduling methods whose complexity is super-exponential.

**Method.** The authors introduce the Fidelity-Optimizing Local Detours (FOLD) heuristic, which iteratively improves paths by merging detours only when distillation boosts the overall fidelity on both branches.

**Model / system.** The model is a quantum network connecting nodes via links characterized by Werner-state entangled pairs. The process involves jointly optimizing path selection, entanglement swapping, and distillation schedules.

**Key observables.** End-to-end fidelity ($F = \langle\Psi^-|ho|\Psi^-angle$), which quantifies the quality of the quantum connection.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The size of the network (number of nodes $n$ and edges $m$), the circuit rank $r(G)$, and the path budget $k$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the ability to evaluate fidelity for swapping and distillation operations, and the heuristic relies on bounding the number of successful merges by the graph's cycle rank.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare fidelity achieved by various scheduling strategies (e.g., purify-then-swap vs. optimal interleaving) and demonstrate the polynomial scaling of the FOLD heuristic compared to exponential exact solvers.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the one-shot routing formulation, contrasts it with rate-based models, develops the mathematical framework for fidelity calculation, introduces the intractable exact solution, and finally proposes and analyzes the polynomial-time FOLD heuristic.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Distributed quantum computation requires many entangled pairs to be available simultaneously, so routing must optimize fidelity from a fixed, short-lived set of network resources rather than the rate of pairs accumulated over time. We formulate this one-shot routing problem for heterogeneous Werner-state links and jointly optimize path selection and the schedule of entanglement swapping and distillation. We show that the common purify-then-swap ordering is not optimal network-wide and that exact schedule enumeration requires $m^{Θ(m)}$ time. We introduce Fidelity-Optimizing Local Detours (FOLD), a heuristic that starts from the highest-fidelity path and merges a detour only when distillation improves on both routes and raises end-to-end fidelity. FOLD runs in polynomial time, recovers almost all of the optimal fidelity on tractable instances, and is four orders of magnitude faster than exact optimization at circuit rank $5$. On the Internet topologies where any strategy improves on shortest-path routing, FOLD achieves the highest mean end-to-end fidelity among the polynomial baselines. We further extend the formulation to links whose fidelities are known only as distributions, where uncertainty, rather than the effort spent routing, limits the fidelity delivered. Through an example of requests competing for the same links, we show that coordination becomes a condition for feasibility, and that a shared path budget controls the fidelity trade-off between them.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes the optimal cost ($\gamma$) associated with gate-cutting, a method for decomposing nonlocal quantum gates. It establishes that $\gamma$ is mathematically linked to the operator-Schmidt spectrum and derives sharp bounding curves showing how five distinct measures of gate nonlocality constrain this cost. The work reveals that no single measure universally determines the optimal cost, providing deep insight into the structure of quantum gate resources.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous quantification of how different measures of nonlocality constrain the fundamental cost of simulating quantum gates is highly relevant for understanding resource theories in quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to determine the relationship between the optimal two-qubit gate-cutting cost ($\gamma$) and various established measures of two-qubit gate nonlocality.

**Main result.** The optimal cost $\gamma$ is shown to be a Rényi-1/2 functional of the operator-Schmidt spectrum, and the study derives sharp lower and upper envelopes connecting $\gamma$ to five distinct nonlocality descriptors.

**Method.** The analysis involves recasting $\gamma$ as a Rényi functional and deriving sharp bounds by analyzing canonical one-parameter families of two-qubit unitaries.

**Model / system.** The system under study is two-qubit unitary gates ($U$), which are parameterized using the Cartan decomposition, restricting the analysis to the non-negative Cartan tetrahedron.

**Key observables.** Optimal QPD Extent ($\gamma$), Entangling power ($e_p$), Gate typicality ($g_t$), Operator entanglement ($E_{op}$), Schmidt strength ($K_{Sch}$), and Maximum product-input concurrence ($C_{max}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The angles ($	heta_1, 	heta_2, 	heta_3$) defining the unitary gate within the Cartan parameters, and the normalized operator-Schmidt spectrum $p$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes invariance of $\gamma$ and the descriptors under local pre- and post-unitaries, allowing restriction to the diagonal unitary form $U_d$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate $\gamma$ versus the five nonlocality descriptors ($e_p, g_t, E_{op}, K_{Sch}$), showing the derived lower and upper bounding envelopes for the optimal gate-cutting cost.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the connection between gate-cutting and the operator-Schmidt spectrum, derives the functional form of $\gamma$, and then systematically derives and compares the sharp lower and upper envelopes imposed by each of the five nonlocality descriptors.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Circuit cutting enables quantum computations to be decomposed into smaller subcircuits at the cost of additional sampling overhead. Gate-cutting provides one such approach by replacing nonlocal gates with quasiprobability decompositions of local operations. Starting from the known optimal two-qubit gate-cutting formula, we derive complete sharp lower and upper envelopes relating the quasiprobability extent $γ$ to five established descriptors: entangling power, gate typicality, operator entanglement, Schmidt strength, and maximum product-input concurrence. We recast $γ$ as a Rényi-$1/2$ functional of the operator-Schmidt spectrum and show how the physical constraints on two-qubit spectra sharpen generic entropy bounds and select a small set of recurring extremal Cartan families. None of the five descriptors generically determines $γ$ alone, but each imposes exact constraints, revealing how substantially the optimal gate-cutting cost can vary between gates with similar nonlocal characteristics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a quantum channel Stein theorem proving that the asymptotic rate for distinguishing between two quantum channels is independent of the testing strategy used (parallel, adaptive, or general). The key finding is that adaptivity offers no asymptotic advantage in this context. The paper rigorously connects hypothesis testing bounds to fundamental quantum divergences.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides fundamental theoretical bounds on quantum channel discrimination, showing that complex causal structures (like general testers) do not offer an asymptotic advantage over simpler, parallel testing schemes.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether different quantum channel testing strategies (parallel, adaptive, general/indefinite causal order) yield different asymptotic advantages when distinguishing between two quantum channels.

**Main result.** It proves that for any fixed error tolerance, all testing strategies achieve the same asymptotic rate, which is the regularized channel relative entropy, demonstrating that adaptivity provides no asymptotic advantage.

**Method.** The analysis uses hypothesis testing theory, relating the achievable rate to the regularized channel relative entropy via continuity proofs of the sandwiched Rényi divergence.

**Model / system.** The system involves finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channels, modeled as Completely Positive Trace-Preserving (CPTP) maps, $N$ and $M$. The testing is performed over $n$ uses of these channels.

**Key observables.** The asymptotic testing rate, $D_{\infty}(N \parallel M)$, and the error probabilities associated with the three tester types (parallel, adaptive, general).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The fixed type-I error tolerance $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ and the number of uses $n 	o \infty$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on establishing the continuity of the regularized sandwiched Rényi channel divergence at order one, and using the fixed-marginal de Finetti theorem for the general tester bound.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the asymptotic equality of testing rates across different strategies (Stein Theorem), to deriving exact one-shot duality relations, and finally establishing the exact strong-converse exponent based on these results.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Distinguishability is a central concept in information theory and extends naturally to quantum systems. This work shows that, for any two finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channels, parallel, adaptive and general testing strategies achieve the same Stein exponent at every fixed type-I error tolerance $ε\in(0,1)$, namely the regularized channel relative entropy. When this rate is finite, any larger type-II exponent forces the probability of correctly accepting the null hypothesis to decay exponentially. Thus, adaptivity provides no asymptotic advantage. The key step is proving the continuity of the regularized sandwiched Rényi channel divergence at order one. We also derive the exact strong-converse exponent for general testers.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes how quantum information, particularly aggregate phases, degrades or becomes 'less recoverable' as it passes through multiple stages of quantum compilation. By formalizing this loss using information-theoretic channels, the authors prove that the compiler's strategy—whether to commit results early or buffer state—imposes a quantifiable resource toll. The key takeaway is the necessity of preserving high-level phase semantics until the final aggregation step to minimize computational overhead.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental, quantitative guidelines for quantum algorithm implementation, directly impacting the resource estimation and feasibility assessment for complex quantum computations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper quantifies the information-theoretic cost associated with compiling high-level quantum structures into low-level gate sequences, specifically focusing on how the choice of compilation representation affects the recoverability of aggregate quantum phases.

**Main result.** The authors establish a formal trade-off showing that early commitment of output information incurs a measurable 'toll' compared to methods that buffer or defer state information, suggesting that preserving phase semantics until the final aggregation step is crucial for efficiency.

**Method.** The work develops a budget-explicit compiler model that charges information-theoretic costs (in bits) for different compilation passes, analyzing the trade-off between committed output ($\overline{A}_p$) and serialized state capacity ($S$).

**Model / system.** The model is applied to quantum compilation, analyzing the process of lowering a high-level structure, such as a commuting layer of phase gates, into a sequence of elementary gates (e.g., Clifford+$T$ words).

**Key observables.** Committed output information ($\overline{A}_p$), serialized crossing-state capacity ($S$), and the specific information toll ($\log_2 inom{m}{k}$) paid by early commitment.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of generators ($m$), approximation tolerance ($\epsilon$), and the number of compilation rounds ($r$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on formalizing the problem via information-theoretic channels and assumes that the physical cost can be mapped to these information-theoretic bounds.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dispersal process of quantum information across compilation rounds and detail the mathematical relationship between the two information currencies ($	ext{S}$ and $	ext{Ap}$) that must be accounted for.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem of representation-dependent recoverability, formalizes the two information channels ($	ext{Ap}$ and $	ext{S}$), derives the core information bound, and then demonstrates this bound using measured tolls from instrumented compilers, concluding with a design rule for optimal compilation pipelines.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Fault-tolerant compilation can disperse high-level structure: schedules split an accumulated phase across rounds, gate synthesis replaces an angle by a Clifford+$T$ word, and randomized compiling spreads rotations over sign-randomized fragments. They preserve the computation but change how cheaply a downstream compiler can recover the aggregate phase data. We formalize this representation-dependent recoverability by charging two channels: output committed before the suffix arrives, and a serialized restart state crossing the cut. For an $r$-round accumulation of a commuting layer with $m$ generators at accuracy $ε$ ($K_ε=Θ(1/ε)$), any $p$-pass compiler correct on every valid stream with failure probability at most $δ$ obeys $\overline{A}_p+(2p-1)S\geq(1-δ)m\log_2 K_ε-h_2(δ)$, where $\overline{A}_p$ is committed output and $S$ is the crossing-state cap. The bound covers compile-time randomized compiling; a memory-capped block compiler attains it within a constant factor, and direct semantic aggregation reaches compact output with logarithmic state.   The two channels are not always interchangeable. A compiler whose committed prefix is executed at the cut pays a toll the state channel never pays: the entropy $\log_2\binom{m}{k}$ of the mask naming which $k$ coordinates it commits early. Compilers that defer or buffer pay none of it. We prove both directions and, with instrumented compilers under a preregistered protocol, measure a per-generator toll matching $\log_2\binom{m}{k}/k$ that vanishes for a public mask and a buffered control.   Under a disclosed fixed-total-error Clifford+$T$ and surface-code model, a materialize-first pipeline costs orders of magnitude more logical $T$ states and spacetime volume than a semantic-first one. Phase semantics should therefore be preserved until aggregation whenever the interface permits.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the optimization landscape of reinforcement learning for algorithmic tasks by mapping it to a spin-glass model. The key finding is that the landscape itself is generally benign, suggesting that training failures are due to traversal issues like diffusive barriers rather than rugged local minima. This has implications for understanding the fundamental limitations of deep learning optimization.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between learning dynamics (RLVR) and the physics of disordered systems (spin glasses) provides a powerful, non-standard lens for understanding optimization in complex machine learning models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the optimization landscape of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) when applied to algorithmic tasks like iterated group multiplication.

**Main result.** The optimization landscape is shown to be benign, meaning local minima are not the primary obstacle; practical difficulties arise instead from diffusive barriers and gradient estimation errors.

**Method.** The authors map the RLVR problem onto an energy-based spin-glass model, allowing for theoretical characterization and comparison with Monte Carlo sampling dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system involves mapping RLVR over myopic tabular policies to a spin-glass model defined over deterministic policies. The task involves sequential token generation for algorithmic problems.

**Key observables.** The structure of the optimization landscape, the existence of local minima, the RLVR-spin-glass gap, and the success rate of learning complex algorithms.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Entropy regulator strength ($eta$), temperature ($	au$), and the degree of input correlation ($k$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis initially relies on the approximation of using myopic tabular policies, and the proof of benignity breaks down with weight tying or input correlations.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare MC stationary distributions against CAVI endpoints, illustrating the effect of the entropy regulator ($	au$) and showing the relationship between reward, entropy, and the spin model.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical mapping from RLVR to spin-glass models, derives variational bounds, compares the convergence dynamics of MC sampling versus RLVR updates, and finally analyzes the impact of input correlations and policy tying on the landscape's traps.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Despite the importance of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), the extent to which it can learn new reasoning capabilities remains debated. Here we study the optimization landscape of RLVR on algorithmic tasks, such as iterated group and quasigroup multiplication. To this end, we map entropy-regularized RLVR over myopic tabular policies onto an energy-based (spin-glass) model over deterministic policies. This mapping upper-bounds what RLVR can achieve, and lets us rigorously characterize the landscape in this tabular setting. We show, both theoretically and experimentally, that for a wide class of models and tasks with uncorrelated inputs, this landscape is benign, containing no local minima that could trap RLVR training. Rather, the practical difficulty of these tasks appears to stem, at least in part, from issues such as diffusive barriers and gradient-estimation error in traversing the landscape. These are genuine obstacles that can prevent a solution from being found, but they are distinct from the landscape itself being rugged. We show that these obstacles can often be mitigated through the choice of entropy regulator. Consistent with this theory, we find that a transformer trained from scratch, using only last-token rewards, successfully learns an algorithmic chain of thought for iterated non-Abelian group multiplications.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops the Moreau-Yosida approximation, $E_\lambda^F$, as a mathematically rigorous and computable substitute for the Entanglement of Formation (EoF). By leveraging convex analysis, the authors establish that $E_\lambda^F$ converges monotonically to the true EoF as the regularization parameter $\lambda 	o 0$. This provides powerful tools for bounding and estimating entanglement in complex quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** Understanding the rigorous mathematical definition and computational tractability of entanglement measures like EoF is fundamental to quantifying quantum resources in quantum information theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the mathematical challenge of defining and approximating the Entanglement of Formation (EoF), a key measure of entanglement in quantum information theory.

**Main result.** It introduces the Moreau-Yosida approximation, $E_\lambda^F$, which is shown to monotonically converge to the true EoF as the regularization parameter $\lambda$ approaches zero.

**Method.** The core method involves applying Moreau-Yosida regularization, a technique from convex analysis, to the definition of EoF to create a sequence of computable, convex approximations.

**Model / system.** The study concerns bipartite quantum systems described by density matrices $ho$ acting on the tensor product of two Hilbert spaces ($\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$).

**Key observables.** Entanglement of Formation ($	ext{EoF}$), the approximation $E_\lambda^F(ho)$, and the difference $|	ext{EoF}(ho) - E_\lambda^F(ho)|$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The regularization parameter $\lambda > 0$, and bounds related to the rank or energy of the marginal states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the global lower semicontinuity of EoF and assumes that the approximation $E_\lambda^F$ is defined via the Moreau envelope structure.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the relative error bound $	ext{bred}(\lambda)$ and $	ext{bre}_{N,E}(\lambda)$ as functions of $\lambda$ for different dimensions and energy levels, showing the convergence rate.

**Paper structure.** The paper first defines the problem using convex analysis, then derives the variational expressions for $E_\lambda^F$, proves its key properties (convexity, monotonicity, subadditivity), and finally analyzes the convergence rate and conditions for exact equality between $E_\lambda^F$ and $E_F$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We describe a family of convex uniformly continuous functions $E^λ_F$, $λ>0$, on the set of states of a bipartite quantum system (consisting of finite-dimensional or infinite-dimensional subsystems), which monotonically increase and converge pointwise to the Entanglement of Formation (EoF) as $λ\to0$. These functions are "nonselective" entanglement monotones defined by the way close to the construction of the Moreau-Yosida regularization (the Moreau envelope) of a convex function on a convex set used in the modern convex analysis. So, we call the functions $E^λ_F$ the Moreau-Yosida approximations of the EoF and describe their equivalent definitions and basic properties.   The semicontinuity bounds for the EoF (presented in [Lob.J.Math., 46(6), 2632-2658]) allow us to obtain easily computable upper bounds on the difference $E_F(ρ)-E^λ_F(ρ)$ for a given state $ρ$. These bounds give easily computable bounds on the rate of uniform convergence of the function $E^λ_F$ to the EoF as $λ\to0^+$ on the sets of states with bounded rank/energy of one of the marginal states.   We also discuss sufficient conditions for the coincidence of $E_F(ρ)$ and $E^λ_F(ρ)$ at a given state $ρ$ for all $λ$ small enough and consider several classes of states for which such coincidence takes place.   The conjectured selective LOCC-monotonicity of the functions $E^λ_F$ and a possible way to prove it are briefly discussed.   Secondary parts of the article are written with the help of ChatGPT-5.6.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves the continuity of the regularized channel Rényi divergence as the parameter $\alpha$ approaches 1. This mathematical result is highly significant as it establishes the computability of the channel relative entropy and yields several major theorems in quantum information theory, such as strong converse bounds for channel discrimination.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental mathematical tools (continuity proofs, computable quantities) for quantifying distinguishability between quantum processes, which is central to quantum communication and computation theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is proving the continuity of the regularized channel Rényi divergence at the limit $\alpha=1$.

**Main result.** The continuity is established, leading to the computability of the channel relative entropy and proving several key theorems, including an exponentially strong converse for channel discrimination.

**Method.** The proof utilizes a variational formula that reduces the divergence to a single-letter optimization problem, followed by a novel spectral confinement technique to establish the limit.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on quantum channels, represented by Completely Positive Trace-Preserving (CPTP) maps, comparing divergences between two such channels, $E$ and $F$.

**Key observables.** Regularized channel Rényi divergence ($D_\alpha^\infty(E\|F)$), channel relative entropy ($D_\infty(E\|F)$), and variational expressions ($C_s(E, F)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The divergence parameter $\alpha$, which is analyzed as $\alpha 	o 1$, and the reparameterization variable $s \in [0, 1)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the Choi matrices $J_E$ and $J_F$ are not pathologically related (e.g., $J_E \ll J_F$) for the quantities to remain bounded.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops by first relating the regularized divergence to variational expressions parameterized by $s$, then proving the continuity of these expressions as $s 	o 0$ (or $\alpha 	o 1$), and finally deriving the consequences for channel discrimination and AEP.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that the regularized channel Rényi divergence is continuous at $α= 1$. As consequences, we establish an exponentially strong converse for channel discrimination, a subchannel-smoothed asymptotic equipartition property, a relative entropy accumulation theorem, and a new proof of the generalized quantum Stein's lemma. Our result further shows that the regularized channel relative entropy is computable. The continuity proof relies on a variational formula that expresses the regularized channel divergence as a single-letter optimization over variables of unrestricted finite dimension. We then establish continuity using a novel spectral confinement technique.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the Ising model on a hyperbolic lattice where boundary effects are dominant. The authors find that conventional methods reveal two distinct temperature scales, $T_{c2}$ and $T^*$, instead of a single critical point. They demonstrate that the true upper thermodynamic transition can only be accessed by applying a specific boundary perturbation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides a detailed case study of how boundary conditions fundamentally alter the identification of thermodynamic critical points in lattice models, which has implications for understanding open quantum systems or finite-size quantum simulations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To study the critical behavior and phase transitions of the Ising model on a hyperbolic lattice where boundary effects are macroscopic and dominate the system's average properties.

**Main result.** The system exhibits two distinct temperature scales ($T_{c2}$ and $T^*$) rather than a single critical point, and the upper thermodynamic transition ($T_{pt}$) can be recovered by perturbing the boundary.

**Method.** Monte Carlo simulations are used extensively, employing techniques like analyzing susceptibility peaks, Binder cumulant crossings, and applying coherent fields to probe different transition regimes.

**Model / system.** The ferromagnetic Ising model is studied on the $\{5, 4\}$ hyperbolic lattice with free boundaries. The geometry ensures that the boundary sites constitute a fixed, macroscopic fraction of the total system volume.

**Key observables.** Susceptibility ($\chi$), Binder cumulant crossings, order-parameter distribution, and the magnetization measured in different spatial regions (Boundary, Bulk, Core, Total).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The lattice geometry ($\{5, 4\}$), the coupling constant $J/k_B$, and the identification of two distinct temperature scales: $T_{c2} \approx 1.48$ and $T^* \approx 1.67$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis must account for the boundary-dependent nature of observables, necessitating finite-size scaling based on the generation index rather than total site count.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the hyperbolic lattice structure and show susceptibility and magnetization curves for different lattice sizes, highlighting the location of the susceptibility maximum and the crossing points for Binder cumulants.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the system by first establishing the boundary-dependent nature of the averages, then identifying the lower transition scale ($T_{c2}$) via susceptibility, followed by locating a pseudocritical scale ($T^*$) using Binder cumulants, and finally recovering the upper transition ($T_{pt}$) via boundary perturbation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

On the $\{5,4\}$ hyperbolic lattice, the outermost generation holds 73\% of the sites at all system sizes, making macroscopic averages strictly boundary-dependent. We study the ferromagnetic Ising model on this geometry with free boundaries by Monte Carlo simulation, demonstrating that conventional observables cease to identify a single critical scale. Instead, the finite lattices are organized by two distinct temperature scales. The susceptibility maximum identifies the lower transition scale at $T_{c2}=1.4782(15)J/k_{B}$ without extrapolation. However, the order-parameter distribution lacks a conventional fixed point at this scale. A distinct pseudocritical scale emerges instead at $T^{*}\simeq1.67(3)$ inside the boundary-sensitive intermediate phase, where Binder cumulant curves cross and effective exponents are compatible with mean-field criticality. Between $T_{c2}$ and $T^{*}$, the interior amplifies boundary fluctuations into induced order. Furthermore, because the volume grows exponentially with depth, finite-size scaling must be formulated in the generation index rather than the total number of sites. The lack of asymptotic power-law convergence in the scaling stretch confirms through an independent observable that $T^{*}$ is a finite-size crossover rather than a thermodynamic fixed point. Finally, by applying a coherent field to the outermost generation alone, we recover the upper thermodynamic transition at $T_{pt}=2.81(1)J/k_{B}$, demonstrating that it remains accessible under an appropriate boundary perturbation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a novel, efficient method for preparing quantum states representing structured classical data by employing the Walsh-Hadamard Transform (WHT) within a Dense-to-Sparse Quantum State Preparation framework. By performing the transformation classically and using the WHT's CNOT-free inverse, the authors eliminate significant gate overhead associated with direct state preparation. This demonstrates that quantum resources scale primarily with the inherent sparsity of the signal in the Walsh domain, making it highly efficient for structured inputs.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on minimizing gate complexity and circuit depth by leveraging specific transforms like WHT is highly relevant to building practical, resource-efficient quantum algorithms for data processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently preparing high-dimensional quantum states corresponding to structured classical data, circumventing the exponential gate overhead of direct state preparation.

**Main result.** By utilizing the Walsh-Hadamard Transform (WHT) within a Dense-to-Sparse Quantum State Preparation (DS-QSP) framework, the authors achieve an efficient, deterministic preparation method with no additional CNOT or circuit-depth overhead in the decompression stage.

**Method.** The method involves a three-stage process: transforming the classical data via WHT (classical compression), preparing the resulting sparse coefficients using a sparse QSP algorithm, and finally reconstructing the state using the CNOT-free inverse WHT.

**Model / system.** The model is based on quantum circuits designed for quantum state preparation (QSP) of amplitude-encoded states. The system utilizes the WHT as the reversible classical transformation, which is implemented quantum mechanically via Hadamard gates.

**Key observables.** Approximation Error (epsilon), total CNOT gate cost, and the trace distance between the prepared and target quantum states.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The required sparsity level (d) relative to the full dimension (N), and the approximation tolerance (e.g., epsilon = 10^-2).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method provides an approximation due to information loss during coefficient thresholding, and its efficiency relies on the input signal having a sparse representation in the Walsh domain.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the general DS-QSP workflow, the quantum circuit structure, and benchmark results showing that structured signals require far fewer coefficients (d) for accurate reconstruction compared to white noise.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the general DS-QSP framework, then proposes and details the specific realization using the WHT. It analyzes the circuit costs, presents numerical results comparing various signal types (sparse vs. white noise), and concludes by discussing the modular nature of the approach.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a hybrid quantum state preparation method based on the Walsh--Hadamard transform within the dense-to-sparse quantum state preparation framework. The method approximately prepares structured classical data in a quantum circuit through an indirect approach. Instead of directly preparing the dense amplitude-encoded state, the method first transforms the classical data into the Walsh domain and prepares only the largest-magnitude coefficients using a sparse state-preparation algorithm. The original state can then be approximately recovered through a parallel layer of Hadamard gates. Since this reconstruction requires no CNOT gates and has circuit depth 1, the proposed method introduces no additional CNOT or circuit-depth overhead, and its quantum preparation cost is determined by the underlying sparse state-preparation algorithm. Numerical results on representative benchmark signals demonstrate that the proposed method enables accurate state preparation for signals admitting sparse or approximately sparse representations in the Walsh domain.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes that momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry is a general weak-coupling route to realizing Pair-Density-Wave (PDW) superconductivity in systems like the TBCB lattice. Using RG and BSE analyses, the authors show this symmetry protects the PDW instability upon doping and allows for the creation of novel topological superconducting phases with quantized Chern numbers.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit connection between a specific lattice symmetry (momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry) and the stabilization of a complex superconducting state (PDW) provides a powerful, symmetry-enforced mechanism for unconventional superconductivity, relevant to correlated materials research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of finding a generic, weak-coupling mechanism to stabilize Pair-Density-Wave (PDW) order, which is often subleading in conventional BCS theory.

**Main result.** Momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry provides a general mechanism that promotes PDW order to a leading weak-coupling instability across a broad doping range, and this mechanism extends to realize topological PDW states in moiré Chern bands.

**Method.** The study employs a combination of Wilsonian Renormalization Group (RG) analysis and the full-component Bethe–Salpeter equation (BSE) analysis to map out competing instabilities.

**Model / system.** The primary model is the Twisted Bilayer Checkerboard (TBCB) lattice, analyzed first with spinless fermions and then extended to spin-1/2 fermions. The analysis focuses on low-energy physics derived from symmetry-protected quadratic band touchings (QBTs).

**Key observables.** Leading instability type (e.g., PDW, QAH, CDW), superconducting gaps ($	ext{s}^{++}, 	ext{s}^{\pm}$), and the topological invariant, the BdG Chern number ($C_{	ext{BdG}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping level ($\mu$), coupling strengths ($g_I, g_{13}, g_{15}$), and the presence/breaking of time-reversal symmetry.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on projecting amplitudes onto exact Bloch states and treating the effective low-energy couplings as the primary variables for RG flow.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate RG source maps showing competing instabilities based on coupling strengths, and the final BSE phase diagram maps the leading ordered phase across varying doping levels.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the general RG framework for instabilities (spinless case) to solving the full-component BSE at finite doping (spin-1/2 case), culminating in the demonstration of topological PDW states.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Pair-density-wave (PDW) order is a superconducting state with a spatially modulated order parameter and is generally subleading to uniform superconductivity within the conventional weak-coupling BCS paradigm. Here, using a twisted bilayer checkerboard-lattice model, we show that momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry provides a generic mechanism that can instead promote PDW order to a leading weak-coupling instability. Combining a controlled Wilsonian renormalization-group analysis at charge neutrality with a finite-doping Bethe--Salpeter analysis, we determine the leading ordering tendencies among various competing instabilities. At charge neutrality, two symmetry-related quadratic band touchings support spin-singlet and spin-triplet PDW instabilities for different attractive interactions, whereas repulsive interactions favor quantum Hall insulators and finite-$\mathbf Q$ density-wave orders. Upon doping, the nonsymmorphic symmetry, together with time reversal, protects the Cooper logarithm in the finite-momentum $\mathbf Q$ pairing channel at generic fillings, allowing PDW order to remain a leading instability over the broad doping range studied. This mechanism extends naturally to moiré Chern bands: by breaking time-reversal symmetry while preserving the nonsymmorphic symmetry and inversion, we obtain a fully gapped topological spin-triplet PDW state with BdG Chern number $C_{\text{BdG}}=8$. Our results establish momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry as a general weak-coupling route to PDW superconductivity, including topological PDW states.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel, highly efficient real-time simulation technique for quantum-dot Josephson junctions by optimizing the bath discretization using a least-squares approach. This method overcomes limitations of previous techniques by treating the numerical broadening parameter independently, leading to massive computational savings. It successfully reproduces key superconducting transport signatures while providing a robust framework for future extensions to interacting systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly advanced, computationally efficient numerical tool for simulating open quantum systems coupled to superconducting leads, which is central to quantum electronics and superconducting circuit QED.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of developing efficient, accurate real-time simulation methods for nonlinear transport in driven superconducting nanostructures.

**Main result.** They introduce a novel real-axis least-squares bath discretization that significantly reduces computational cost while accurately recovering established superconducting transport phenomena.

**Method.** The authors extend the driven Liouville-von Neumann approach by formulating the bath discretization as a constrained nonlinear least-squares optimization problem.

**Model / system.** The system is a noninteracting quantum dot Josephson junction coupled to superconducting leads, modeled using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism in the Nambu basis.

**Key observables.** Current-phase relations (CPR), multiple-Andreev-reflection (MAR) structure, quasiparticle-trapping oscillations, and Shapiro locking amplitudes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The independently calibrated numerical broadening parameter ($\gamma$), the ratio $\kappa \simeq w_{	ext{bath}}\gamma_{	ext{eff}}$, and the joint refinement path $(\gamma 	o 0, N_b 	o \infty)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The dot is treated as noninteracting ($U=0$), and the method relies on careful gauge selection (hopping-phase gauge) when implementing damping in the DLvN framework.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the system setup, the locking map on the LS-32 bath, and comparisons of static CPRs against continuum benchmarks.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the Hamiltonian model (Section II.A), the superconducting DLvN formulation (Section II.B), and the core least-squares bath framework (Section II.C), followed by extensive validation of observables and comparisons with other methods in Section III.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Efficient real-time methods are essential for resolving transient coherence and nonlinear transport in driven superconducting nanostructures. Such simulations remain challenging because finite representations of the BCS continuum generate recurrences, while the damping used to suppress them smears gap-edge structure and artificially shortens coherent lifetimes; finite-broadening regularization of the gap-edge singularity likewise imposes a lifetime-resolution floor. Here we extend the driven Liouville--von Neumann approach to superconducting reservoirs---a noninteracting quantum dot with Bogoliubov--de Gennes leads---building an explicit-Hamiltonian framework that hosts a family of bath discretizations (uniform and Gaussian baselines and a new real-axis least-squares recipe, with mode energies, spectral weights, and mode-resolved dampings optimized jointly under gap-aware constraints)---making the broadening an independently calibrated numerical parameter whose leading long-time effect extrapolates controllably along the joint ($γ\to0$, $N_b\to\infty$) refinement path while cutting computational cost by over an order of magnitude versus the high-resolution DLvN reference. The compressed baths recover established current-phase relations, multiple-Andreev-reflection structure, quasiparticle-trapping oscillations, and integer and fractional Shapiro locking; the lifetime analysis yields the parameter-free leading-order relation $κ\simeq w_{\mathrm{bath}}γ_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and resolves damping-induced decay rates below the resolution scale of a previous finite-broadening calculation. As an explicit Hamiltonian reservoir representation, the framework generalizes naturally to multiterminal normal--superconducting geometries and offers a route toward interacting impurity solvers, while finite-gap strong-drive locking amplitudes mark its present quantitative boundary.

</details>

**Summary.** This work delivers a comprehensive data package and theoretical framework for studying strongly chirped dissipative solitons governed by the cubic-quintic Ginzburg-Landau equation. It details methods to calculate spectral properties and map out the stability boundaries under quantum noise in both normal and anomalous dispersion regimes. The resource is valuable for researchers needing to benchmark numerical simulations in nonlinear wave physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed mathematical machinery, involving spectral analysis and stability mapping under noise, is highly relevant to open quantum systems and nonlinear wave dynamics, bridging quantum optics and nonlinear PDEs.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper provides comprehensive datasets and analytical tools to reproduce complex spectral and stability analyses for strongly chirped dissipative solitons.

**Main result.** The analysis characterizes the existence, spectral properties, and quantum-noise stability regions of these solitons across normal and anomalous dispersion regimes.

**Method.** The study employs adiabatic theory, stationary-phase approximations, uniformization techniques, and stochastic propagation simulations to analyze the nonlinear evolution.

**Model / system.** The system is governed by the cubic-quintic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation (CGLE), modeling dissipative solitons in nonlinear wave propagation.

**Key observables.** Stationary-phase spectra, windowed first-order coherence functions, quantum-noise stability maps, and energy ($	ext{ENGD}(	ilde{\chi})$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dispersion regimes (Normal/Anomalous), normalized control parameters ($\Sigma, \delta C$), and the chirp parameter ($	ilde{\chi}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the adiabatic approximation (large-chirp limit) and the use of finite-time stochastic classification for stability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 maps stability regions in parameter space under quantum noise; Figure 2 compares the analytical soliton profile against its noisy, perturbed realization.

**Paper structure.** The structure moves from defining the CGLE and its parameters, through deriving analytical approximations for energy and spectral features (SPA, uniformization), to analyzing the stability via stochastic simulation and presenting the final data repository.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

This data article provides the datasets, symbolic derivations, and scripts used to reproduce master diagrams, stationary-phase spectra, windowed first-order coherence functions, and quantum-noise stability maps for strongly chirped dissipative solitons of the cubic-quintic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in normal and anomalous group-delay dispersion regimes. The repository includes node-regularized normal-dispersion spectra and energies; small-parameter expansions of the branch roots; cavity-map gain-loss update relations; Airy uniformization at the normal-dispersion spectral edge; anomalous-dispersion spectra and coherence calculations; and processed tables for plotting and stability analysis. OriginLab projects are accompanied by open-format .csv/.txt numerical tables to support reuse without proprietary plotting software. Data and code repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22690899.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the fundamental physics governing mechanical coupling between localized cavities and propagating waveguides in phononic crystals. Using both finite-element simulations and experimental measurements on GaAs, the authors establish that the coupling strength is predominantly determined by the spatial overlap of the involved vibrational modes. This work provides critical design guidelines for realizing solid-state quantum networks based on phononic interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, quantitative design rules—namely, maximizing spatial mode overlap—for engineering solid-state quantum interconnects using phononics, which is crucial for building scalable quantum networks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is understanding and controlling the coupling strength between localized mechanical modes (cavities) and propagating phononic modes (waveguides) within phononic crystals for use in scalable on-chip quantum networks.

**Main result.** The coupling strength is found to be primarily governed by the spatial overlap between the displacement fields of the isolated cavity and waveguide modes. Experimentally, a clear resonance was observed in the photoluminescence broadening matching simulation predictions.

**Method.** The study employs a combination of finite-element simulations (FEM) to model coupling strength via avoided crossings and experimental measurements using embedded quantum dots (QDs) as local mechanical field probes.

**Model / system.** The system involves phononic crystals realized in GaAs, featuring snowflake-type cavities coupled to a waveguide. The interaction mediates coupling between solid-state qubits (like QDs) via mechanical excitations (phonons).

**Key observables.** Coupling strength (quantified by frequency splitting $\Delta f$), spatial overlap integral ($\eta$), and spectral broadening of photoluminescence emission.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Lattice constant ($a$), cavity radius ($r$), waveguide group velocity ($v_g$), and the spatial overlap integral $\eta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial analysis focuses on the leading-order behavior governed by spatial mode overlap, with deviations attributed to Bloch-phase effects and hybridization.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the geometry of the coupled system, show calculated dispersion relations revealing avoided crossings, and present experimental false-color plots showing QD emission modulation mapping out the phononic band gap and cavity resonances.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by simulating the coupling using FEM, showing the dependence on spatial overlap. It then presents experimental evidence by measuring QD photoluminescence resonance in a fabricated GaAs membrane, confirming the theoretical predictions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Phononic crystal platforms provide a promising route toward scalable on-chip quantum networks, where mechanical excitations mediate interactions between solid-state qubits. A key building block of such architectures is the cavity-waveguide system, in which localized mechanical modes couple to propagating phononic modes. However, a quantitative understanding of the mechanisms governing this coupling remains incomplete. In this work, we investigate the interaction between localized modes of snowflake-type phononic crystal cavities and a phononic crystal waveguide using finite-element simulations and experimental measurements. We show that the coupling strength is primarily governed by the spatial overlap between the displacement fields of the corresponding isolated cavity and waveguide modes. After accounting for the effective-mass dependence of the normalized cavity displacement amplitude, we establish a strong correlation between the spatial overlap and the interaction strength across a wide range of mode combinations. Deviations from this leading-order behavior are associated with Bloch-phase effects, variations in waveguide group velocity, and intrinsic hybridization of waveguide modes. Furthermore, we provide experimental evidence for cavity-waveguide coupling in a GaAs phononic crystal membrane by observing a clear resonance in the spectral broadening of the photoluminescence emission from an embedded quantum dot, which serves as a local probe of the mechanical field. The observed resonance at approximately 398 MHz is in good agreement with the corresponding cavity resonance near 395 MHz predicted by finite-element simulations. Our results identify spatial mode overlap as a leading-order design parameter for cavity-waveguide coupling and provide practical guidelines for controlling interactions between localized and propagating modes in phononic crystal structures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes how circularly polarized light generates a rectified orbital magnetization in electron-hole bilayers, a phenomenon requiring inherent asymmetry between the electron and hole layers. The authors develop a comprehensive theoretical framework covering both weak-coupling (Drude) and strong-coupling (excitonic) regimes. The findings confirm that asymmetry is key to observing this magnetization, providing insights into tunable spintronic materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The interplay between light-matter interaction, orbital magnetism, and the crossover between semiclassical (Drude) and strongly correlated (excitonic) regimes is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the light-induced rectified orbital magnetization in electron-hole bilayers, specifically addressing how structural asymmetry prevents the exact cancellation of electron and hole contributions.

**Main result.** The induced magnetization is non-zero due to electron-hole asymmetry, yielding a finite response in both the weak-coupling Drude limit and the strong-coupling excitonic regime.

**Method.** The authors employ a combination of semiclassical Drude modeling for weak coupling and a quantum mechanical hydrogenic model for strong coupling, analyzing the response using time-dependent perturbation theory.

**Model / system.** The system is an electron-hole bilayer, modeled using transition-metal dichalcogenide platforms. The Hamiltonian is treated in two limits: a two-component Drude model for weak coupling, and a hydrogenic model with a Rytova-Keldysh interaction for interlayer excitons.

**Key observables.** Orbital IFE-induced magnetization ($\langle M angle$), carrier dynamics, and the drag resistivity ($ho_D$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Effective mass asymmetry ($m_e/m_h$), interlayer coupling strength ($\gamma$), and the driving frequency ($\omega$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Drude model is limited to weakly correlated carriers, and the strong-coupling analysis assumes an effective hydrogenic potential.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically shows the driving mechanism emphasizing asymmetry; Figure 2 illustrates how interlayer drag couples carrier trajectories, reducing orbital radii.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from the general problem statement, develops the weak-coupling Drude description, analyzes the crossover via drag resistivity, and finally tackles the strong-coupling regime using a quantum excitonic model.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Circularly polarized light can rectify orbital motion into a static magnetization through the inverse Faraday effect (IFE), but in electron-hole bilayers the electron and hole contributions cancel exactly when their properties are equivalent. We show that electron-hole bilayers in transition-metal dichalcogenide platforms avoid this cancellation through effective-mass asymmetry alone, and that the surviving orbital IFE is sensitive to interlayer coupling. In the weak-coupling regime, a two-component Drude description yields an induced magnetization of order one Bohr magneton per carrier for representative terahertz driving. In the strong-coupling regime, where the carriers bind into interlayer excitons, we treat the relative motion using a hydrogenic model with a Rytova-Keldysh interaction and obtain a reduced but finite response. We give closed-form expressions that allow estimates across a broad parameter range and identify where the response is largest.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work investigates the possibility of Bose-Einstein Condensation in the Higgs collective mode of a superconductor when externally pumped. By deriving a microscopic Hamiltonian and analyzing the resulting bosonic gas, the authors establish density bounds for condensation and confirm that realistic pumping mechanisms can achieve the necessary conditions for BEC.

**Why it may be interesting.** It connects concepts from superconductivity (Higgs/Goldstone modes) to the physics of ultracold atomic gases (BEC), providing a concrete, solid-state realization of a bosonic condensate.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine if an optically pumped gas of Higgs modes in a superconductor can undergo Bose-Einstein Condensation (BEC).

**Main result.** The paper finds that a density window exists where BEC is possible, and the expected pumped mode density is compatible with condensation for realistic material parameters.

**Method.** The authors derive a microscopic Hamiltonian for the coupled Higgs-Goldstone-electron system and analyze the resulting bosonic gas dynamics using mean-field theory and density calculations.

**Model / system.** The system is a superconductor, modeled by starting from the BCS Hamiltonian and deriving a Hamiltonian for the collective Higgs (amplitude) and Goldstone (phase) modes. The Higgs subsystem is treated as a weakly interacting Bose gas.

**Key observables.** Higgs mode density ($n_P$), BEC critical density ($n_{BEC}$), and density collapse limit ($n_{col}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fermi energy ($\epsilon_F$), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), and the coupling constant derived from external electromagnetic fields.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Higgs mode is treated as a bosonic gas, and the analysis relies on approximations like the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) when deriving the dispersion relations.

**Figures summary.** Not specified.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives the Hamiltonian for the collective modes, calculates the dispersion relations for Higgs and Goldstone modes, and finally applies this theory to establish the necessary density window for non-equilibrium BEC.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Collective modes in a superconductor correspond to fluctuations in the amplitude (Higgs mode) or the phase (Goldstone mode) of the order parameter. Starting from the BCS Hamiltonian, we derive a microscopic Hamiltonian for the coupled Higgs-Goldstone-electron system that contains all interactions among these degrees of freedom. The Higgs subsystem is a weakly interacting Bose gas: Higgs modes experience a mutual attraction mediated by the virtual exchange of Bogoliubov quasi-particle pairs. They also interact with external electromagnetic-fields with a coupling constant that we derive explicitly. We use this theory to examine whether an optically pumped gas of Higgs modes can undergo Bose-Einstein condensation. We identify a density window, bounded below by the equilibrium condensation criterion and above by collapse due to the attractive interaction, in which condensation can occur and we derive the expected density of Higgs-modes due to external pumping. This pumping depends crucially on non-parabolic corrections to the electron dispersion around the Fermi-energy. We show that the pumped mode density is compatible with condensation for realistic material parameters. We suggest possible experimental signatures of this non-equilibrium condensate.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the local structural disorder in natural sanidine using single-crystal diffuse scattering. By combining 3D-PDF analysis with detailed force-field and Monte Carlo simulations, the authors developed a model showing that the observed anisotropic scattering arises from correlated framework distortions driven primarily by local K/Na ion ordering. This provides a detailed picture of coupled occupational and displacive disorder in complex aluminosilicate frameworks.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state crystallography, the methodology of modeling complex, coupled local disorder using statistical mechanics (Monte Carlo) and energy minimization techniques is relevant to understanding many-body interactions in disordered quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to understand the local structural correlations associated with chemical disorder in natural sanidine, which cannot be resolved using only average-structure analysis.

**Main result.** The diffuse scattering features, including characteristic bowtie-like patterns, are successfully reproduced by a model combining correlated K/Na occupational short-range order with anisotropic framework distortions.

**Method.** The research combines single-crystal diffuse scattering experiments with advanced computational techniques, including 3D-PDF analysis, force-field calculations, and Monte Carlo modeling.

**Model / system.** The physical system is natural sanidine, an alkali feldspar. The model incorporates chemically constrained Al/Si distributions and local framework relaxations driven by the occupancy of K and Na ions.

**Key observables.** Anisotropic diffuse features, particularly bowtie-like intensity distributions in reciprocal space, and oscillatory patterns in the 3D-PDF.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis focuses on the coupling between occupational disorder (K/Na) and displacive disorder (framework distortions).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes that the Al/Si disorder follows Löwenstein's rule, and that the primary source of diffuse scattering is the coupled disorder between alkali occupancy and framework relaxation.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare experimental and modeled diffuse scattering patterns in various planes (hk0, h0l, 0kl) and show the 3D-PDF, illustrating the anisotropic nature of the disorder.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of average structure analysis, then applying 3D-PDF and force-field methods to characterize the disorder, and finally constructing a comprehensive model that successfully reproduces the key anisotropic diffuse scattering features.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Natural sanidine commonly preserves metastable chemical disorder at ambient conditions, but the local structural correlations associated with this disorder remain poorly understood due to a reliance on average-structure analysis alone. Here, we investigate single-crystal diffuse scattering in a natural sanidine from Drachenfels, Germany, with consistent observations across additional samples from Laacher See, Germany, and Vesuvio, Italy. The diffraction data reveal pronounced anisotropic diffuse features, including characteristic bowtie-like intensity distributions in reciprocal space. To resolve the origin of these features, we combine three-dimensional difference pair distribution function (3D-$Δ$PDF) analysis with force-field calculations and Monte Carlo modelling. The 3D-$Δ$PDF shows correlated deviations from the average structure and indicates a strong coupling between occupational and displacive disorder. Force-field calculations demonstrate that the aluminosilicate framework responds strongly to the local alkali occupancy, with the largest structural variation occurring along the $a$ direction. Guided by these observations, we construct a disorder model in which K/Na occupational short-range order is combined with chemically constrained Al/Si distributions and local framework relaxations. The model reproduces the main experimental diffuse-scattering features and shows that the bowtie-like diffuse scattering arises from correlated framework distortions driven primarily by local K/Na order.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a general, microscopic theory for calculating extrinsic disorder contributions to the orbital Hall effect in multiband solids. By solving a quantum kinetic equation for the wavevector-off-diagonal density matrix, the authors show that disorder effects are significant and cannot be simply scaled by disorder strength. The results provide quantitative predictions for systems like the massive Dirac cone, advancing the field of orbitronics.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter transport, the rigorous development of a quantum kinetic equation for off-diagonal density matrices and the inclusion of higher-order scattering terms provide a general, advanced theoretical framework applicable to open quantum systems dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a microscopic theory to calculate extrinsic contributions to the full orbital current, addressing limitations in conventional orbital Hall effect calculations.

**Main result.** Disorder-generated extrinsic corrections are generically comparable to the intrinsic current, and for a massive Dirac cone, the total current is found to be exactly twice the quantum correction.

**Method.** The theory solves the quantum kinetic equation for the wavevector-off-diagonal density matrix, incorporating band-structure, side-jump, and skew-scattering terms within the non-crossing approximation.

**Model / system.** The theory is applied to general multiband solids, specifically modeling a massive Dirac cone and a variant with particle-hole-symmetry-breaking terms.

**Key observables.** Orbital angular momentum (OAM) current, orbital conductivity ($\sigma_{yx}$), intrinsic current ($j_{int}$), and extrinsic contributions (Born, skew, side-jump).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Disorder strength ($	au$), Fermi energy ($E_F$), and the symmetry-breaking parameter ($\kappa$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes dilute, identical, short-range scalar impurities and utilizes the non-crossing approximation for collision terms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate orbital conductivity vs. Fermi energy for the massive Dirac cone model, showing intrinsic, extrinsic, and total conductivity, and also show the disorder scaling of the extrinsic orbital current.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem by noting the need for a full evaluation of the orbital current, develops the kinetic equation for the off-diagonal density matrix, calculates the various scattering terms (Born, skew, side-jump), and presents results for specific models like the massive Dirac cone.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The orbital Hall effect (OHE) underpins the emerging field of orbitronics. A complete quantum-mechanical evaluation of the usual orbital-current operator must retain all matrix elements of the position operator, including its band-diagonal differential part; intrinsic calculations based on this full evaluation can differ by orders of magnitude from the conventional truncation. A relaxation-time estimate of disorder effects on the full current has been reported, but a microscopic treatment of extrinsic scattering has remained unavailable because the position operator requires wavevector-off-diagonal density-matrix elements. Here we develop such a theory by solving the quantum kinetic equation for the wavevector-off-diagonal density matrix, including band-structure, field-corrected side-jump, and skew-scattering terms within the non-crossing approximation. We apply the theory to a massive Dirac cone and to the same model with a particle-hole-symmetry-breaking quadratic term. Disorder-generated contributions of order $τ^0$ are generically comparable to the intrinsic current in the metallic regime and cannot be separated from it by simple disorder-strength scaling. For the bare massive Dirac cone the surviving non-crossing extrinsic correction cancels the conventional intrinsic value and leaves a total current exactly twice the quantum correction, whereas particle-hole asymmetry activates conventional skew scattering for disorder with a non-zero third moment, which dominates in sufficiently clean samples. The wavevector-off-diagonal construction is independent of the two-band model and provides a general route to disorder corrections for position-dependent observables in multiband solids.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores topological superconductivity in extended Kitaev models by introducing power-law interactions and multiple sub-lattices. The authors demonstrate that long-range pairing and hopping induce unique topological features, leading to an unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence. This provides deeper insight into how dimensionality and interaction decay affect Majorana zero mode physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The findings on unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence and the persistence of Majorana modes despite changes in the winding number are highly relevant for understanding topological superconductivity in engineered quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates topological superconducting phases in extended Kitaev models that incorporate long-range (LR) hopping and superconductivity, focusing on the role of sub-lattices and power-law interactions.

**Main result.** The model exhibits unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence, where LR superconductivity promotes massive Dirac (Majorana zero) modes, and the winding number can take half-integer values depending on the sub-lattice parity.

**Method.** The analysis involves constructing generalized SSH-Kitaev models and calculating topological invariants, such as the winding number, in both the thermodynamic limit and for finite-size systems.

**Model / system.** The system is based on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH)-Kitaev model, extended to include mono-, bi-, and tri-partite sub-lattices. The Hamiltonian features power-law decay ($r^{-\epsilon}, r^{-\alpha}$) for both hopping and superconducting pairing terms.

**Key observables.** Topological invariants (winding number $W_r$), Mid-Gap Modes (MDMs), and the existence/location of critical lines.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Power-law decay exponents ($\alpha, \epsilon$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the number of sub-lattices (even vs. odd).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares results from the thermodynamic limit (momentum space) to finite-size systems (real space), noting discrepancies in the boundary correspondence.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically represent the three SSH-Kitaev models and show winding number phase diagrams illustrating how superconducting/hopping conditions alter the topological phase boundaries.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the SSH-Kitaev model across different sub-lattice structures (SSH1, SSH2, SSH3), comparing the effects of LR hopping versus LR superconductivity on the topological phase diagram and the resulting boundary conditions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The power-law profile of hopping and superconductivity introduces rich critical phenomena that are not possible to explore in the nearest-neighbor models. Having this in mind, we construct the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH)-Kitaev model with mono-, bi-, and tri-partite sub-lattices where superconductivity [hopping] is of power-law Kitaev [SSH] type. The long-range (LR) superconductivity can alone gap out the zero-momentum critical line while LR hopping alters the finite-momentum critical line. There exists open-ended critical line at vanishing superconducting gap on the phase diagram for all versions of the SSH-Kitaev model. Interestingly, LR superconductivity (hopping) promotes massive Dirac (Majorana zero) modes, while in a finite-size system, their emergence in open boundary conditions is caused by the bulk gap of the anti-periodic Hamiltonian in momentum space. This indicates an unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence for power-law models as compared to what is seen in the short-range models. Importantly, the thermodynamic phase boundaries are correctly reproduced by the above unconventional correspondence. Intriguingly, an even (odd) number of sub-lattices yields an integer (half-integer) winding number while the massive Dirac modes continue to survive irrespective of the sub-lattice profile as long as there exists LR pairing only.

</details>
