**Summary.** This work investigates superconducting spin valves to separate the contributions of Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. By measuring in-plane conductance anisotropy, the authors successfully quantified the D-SOC contribution, linking it to structural defects. This provides a practical method for engineering superconducting spintronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to use superconducting transport measurements to isolate and quantify specific microscopic couplings like D-SOC is a powerful tool for condensed matter physics, providing insights into symmetry breaking and electronic structure relevant to quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to experimentally and theoretically disentangle the contributions of Rashba (R-SOC) and Dresselhaus (D-SOC) spin-orbit coupling components in superconducting spintronic junctions.

**Main result.** The in-plane conductance anisotropy was successfully analyzed, revealing a quantifiable 5% contribution of D-SOC, which was linked to periodic lattice mismatch defects at the interfaces.

**Method.** The research combines low-bias conductance anisotropy measurements in epitaxial superconducting spin valves with a theoretical model incorporating distinct R-SOC and D-SOC terms.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an epitaxial Fe/MgO/V/MgO/Fe/Co junction, functioning as a superconducting spin valve. The analysis relies on modeling transport phenomena governed by SOC anisotropy.

**Key observables.** In-plane low-bias conductance anisotropy ($\Delta G_N(\varphi)$) and normalized zero-bias conductance anisotropy ($\Delta[G(0)/G_N](\varphi)$) as functions of angle, temperature, and magnetic field.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), in-plane magnetic field ($H$), and the ratio of D-SOC to R-SOC ($eta/\alpha$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed anisotropy is dominated by SOC effects and that the theoretical model accurately captures the physics of Andreev reflections in the superconducting state.

**Figures summary.** Figures show $G$ vs $V$ curves, angular dependence of conductance anisotropy ($\Delta G_N$ and $\Delta[G(0)/G_N]$), and STEM images confirming interfacial lattice mismatch defects.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the physical system and the need to separate R-SOC and D-SOC contributions. It details the experimental measurements of conductance anisotropy, applies a theoretical model, and concludes by quantifying the D-SOC contribution and discussing implications for superconducting pairing.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) plays a central role in modern condensed matter physics and is crucial for the development of spin-based devices and quantum technologies. In particular, the interplay between Rashba SOC (R-SOC), arising from structural inversion asymmetry, and Dresselhaus SOC (D-SOC), due to bulk inversion asymmetry, significantly influences spin coherence and manipulation in two-dimensional and topological systems. Disentangling these SOC components is essential for spintronics, superconducting spintronics, or topological superconductivity. In this study, we experimentally investigate in-plane low-bias conductance anisotropy in epitaxial Fe/MgO/V/MgO/Fe/Co junctions under varying temperature and magnetic field conditions. By applying a theoretical model that accounts for distinct R-SOC and D-SOC contributions, we interpret the observed anisotropy as a reliable method to disentangle these effects. Comparison between experiment and theory reveals a 5 % contribution of D-SOC to total SOC, attributed to periodic interfacial lattice mismatch defects confirmed by high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Our findings offer a practical approach to isolate interfacial SOC components in superconducting spintronic systems with implications for engineering in spintronic and quantum devices, and provide further evidence of superconducting spin-triplet pairing in Fe/MgO/V-based superconductor/ferromagnet heterostructures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces a novel nonlinear valley Hall effect driven by the valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD) in materials with time-reversal-invariant valleys (TRIVs). The authors theoretically prove this effect is symmetry-protected and demonstrate its feasibility using first-principles calculations on strained $	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$. It provides a pathway for controlling valley-specific transport responses in 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter transport, the concept of Berry curvature dipoles and nonlinear responses relates to geometric phases and topological invariants, which are key concepts in advanced quantum physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates a previously unexplored nonlinear valley Hall effect (VHE) mechanism driven by the valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD). It specifically focuses on systems where valleys are related by crystal symmetry rather than time-reversal symmetry.

**Main result.** The vBCD-induced nonlinear VHE is forbidden in conventional time-reversal-connected valleys but is supported in time-reversal-invariant valley (TRIV) systems. The effect allows for selective control between valley and charge Hall responses.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical symmetry analysis (searching 80 layer groups) with first-principles calculations on a concrete material example ($	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$) and proposes nonlocal transport measurements.

**Model / system.** The system under study is a 2D nonmagnetic material exhibiting two valleys ($	ext{V}_1, 	ext{V}_2$) in the conduction band, specifically focusing on TRIV systems. The analysis uses symmetry groups and effective models derived from $k \cdot p$ theory.

**Key observables.** Nonlinear VHE current ($j_v$), nonlinear charge Hall response, and nonlocal voltage signals ($	ext{V}_{3\omega}^{	ext{NL}} \propto ho^3$, $	ext{V}_{4\omega}^{	ext{NL}} \propto ho^4$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Relaxation time ($	au$), the valley Berry curvature dipole ($\Lambda_v$), and the driving electric field direction relative to $\Lambda_v$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the Fermi level is near the band edge and focuses on the two relevant valleys. The vBCD mechanism is necessary but not sufficient for the effect.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the vBCD mechanism in TRIV systems and show the dependence of the nonlinear VHE conductivity ($\chi_v$) on the angle between the driving field and $\Lambda_v$.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical problem, develops the theoretical framework using symmetry constraints to identify candidate materials, derives the nonlinear transport equations, and validates the predictions using both model calculations and a concrete material example ($	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Valley Hall effect is a signature effect in the field of valleytronics, and recent studies have pushed this effect into the nonlinear regime. Here, we reveal a previously unexplored type of nonlinear valley Hall effect which arises from a valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD) mechanism. We show this nonlinear valley Hall effect is forbidden for conventional time-reversal-connected valleys, but is supported in the class of valleytronic systems featuring time-reversal-invariant valleys. The candidate layer groups and detailed symmetry constraints on vBCD are obtained. It shows the nonlinear valley Hall response, as well as the nonlinear charge Hall response, can be well controlled by tuning the driving field direction. We demonstrate our proposal in an effective model study and in a concrete material example, strained Nb$_{3}$SBr$_{7}$, by first-principles calculations. The nonlocal transport signature of this vBCD induced nonlinear valley Hall effect is also discussed.

</details>
